evidence_items.summary: Deploying LLM-based analytics agents in enterprise settings requires evaluation frameworks that can reliably detect failures across complex, multi-tool workflows. We present a three-phase comparative study of three evaluation frameworks, each representing a distinct evaluation paradigm (trace-based LLM judging, text-only LLM judging with red-teaming, and deterministic heuristics), applied to two analytics agents in a controlled research setting using frozen execution traces. Phase 1 quantifies evaluation harness stability through repeated measurements, finding that 97% of configurations meet the stability threshold and that stability patterns are agent-independent. Phase 2 measures known risk detection on 72 ground-truth test cases, where the trace-based framework achieves the best precision-recall balance (F1=0.90) while text-only evaluation matches on recall but generates 5x more false alarms. Phase 3 evaluates unknown risk discovery, uncovering 24 novel failures with zero overlap between functional testing and security red-teaming. Our results demonstrate that (1) the information available to the evaluation harness determines evaluation quality, (2) functional and security evaluation are complementary, and (3) LLM-based evaluation harnesses surface subtle errors that human reviewers miss. We recommend a two-framework strategy: trace-based evaluation for functional assessment and adversarial red-teaming for security validation.
evidence_items.title: Comparative Analysis of Agent Evaluation Frameworks: Stability, Detection, and Discovery in Enterprise Analytics Agents

evidence_items.summary: We describe our solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge: 100 long-horizon household tasks in the OmniGibson simulator. We placed 9th on the final leaderboard, the only independent team in the top 10. The core of the solution is a single vision-language-action (VLA) model, one checkpoint for all 100 tasks, built on our 1st-place 2025 solution, which is based on $\pi_{0.5}$. On the 50 tasks shared with 2025, its Q rises from 0.260 to 0.371; across all 100 tasks it scores 0.392. Our main conclusion from 2025 was that the model was undertrained, so most of the 2026 work went into training the model for longer, optimizing some training parameters, making each training step slightly faster and reducing the gradient noise: a migration from 50 to 100 tasks (semantic stages built from the demonstrations' skill annotations, task and stage embeddings of new tasks warm-started from similar old ones, and a 21-dimensional action space matching the teleoperation controls); variance-reduced multi-sample flow matching with a simple noise-vs-compute model that picks the number of action-expert samples per observation without ablations; and a 200k-step training run, about one pass over the 211M frames of the demonstrations. A cloud evaluation infrastructure keeps a shared record with provenance, episode diagnostics and restorable simulator states, and runs six simulators on one GPU together faster than real time. On top of the learned policy, 14 tasks are routed to a GPT-6 Astra coding agent that controls the robot through observation and motion tools, starting every episode from a frozen copy of its own practice session on training instances. Across these 14 tasks, Astra's mean Q is 0.639, against 0.108 for the learned policy. The public submission included only part of the Astra results and scored 0.446 Q with 27.3% full-task success.
evidence_items.title: One Policy for 100 Household Tasks: Our Solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge

evidence_items.summary: Formal world models can support planning, verification, and safety reasoning, but constructing them from open-ended natural-language situations is difficult, particularly in multi-agent settings where several formalizations may be plausible. We study whether five LLMs can generate such world models as partially observable stochastic games and whether mechanical validity is sufficient to establish that the resulting model faithfully represents the intended decision problem. We introduce a benchmark of 44 scenarios spanning game, situational, and cultural settings and evaluate generated world models along three dimensions: mechanical validity, reference-relative structural agreement, and semantic criteria. Across three empirical tracks, we analyze 410 first-pass generations. In the reference-backed game track, 134/135 generated world models pass a strict mechanical audit, yet mean permutation-invariant structural F1 is only 0.366, with just 28/134 mechanically valid models exactly matching the authored reference. In the cultural track, explicitly naming the country changes the generated structural representation for most LLMs while producing only small changes in automated semantic scores. These results show that executability is a necessary but insufficient criterion for LLM-generated world models: models that are mechanically valid can still differ substantially in the structure used by downstream neuro-symbolic reasoning and planning.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating LLM-Generated World Models for Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Users often complain that AI assistants such as ChatGPT are getting worse. Some versions do change, but human evaluation leaves a second possibility untested: the people judging may change. We separate the two on Chatbot Arena, a public platform where people compare answers from two anonymous large language models (LLMs) and pick the better one or say both are bad. We study 1,260,967 blind votes cast from May 2023 to August 2024 on pairs of models whose versions are fixed: dated vendor snapshots and models with fixed open weights. For the same pair of unchanged models, the share of votes saying "both are bad" rises by 1.71 percentage points a month on a mean of 17.1%, and by 1.91 points a month in 2024. In fourteen pairs observed often in both 2023 and 2024, it rose in every one, from 15.5% to 23.3%. The ranking does not trend: in 2024, the stronger model's share of decisive votes is flat. The rise holds within the same voter and on the same pair, and across arrival cohorts from their first recorded vote. It holds with prompt controls, in every major language, for dated vendor snapshots, open-weight models and models with stable answer length, and between interface changes. The drift is shared across models: month effects estimated from other models' pairs remove it from each model's own pairs. Platform-wide, the average model would be expected to score 78% against the 2023 average, yet the share of "both are bad" votes ended near where it began. The pattern fits a standard that follows the category's progress, so a product that stands still is judged as declining. Absolute verdicts on AI drifted while relative comparisons held steady, an evaluation drift that matters for LLM leaderboards and for the human feedback used to train models.
evidence_items.title: AI Isn't Getting Dumber, We're Getting Pickier: Rising Standards in Human Evaluation of Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Motivation: Gene regulatory networks (GRNs) capture the underlying interactions through which transcription factors (TFs) regulate genes. Based on gene expression data, existing GRN inference approaches generally fall into two categories: graph-based methods, which model the GRN as a whole graph, and pairwise-based methods, which decompose the GRN into individual TF-target gene pairs for modeling. However, each approach exhibits limitations that are precisely the strengths of its counterpart. Graph-based methods tend to overfit due to their reliance on a single training graph, whereas pairwise-based methods benefit from abundant TF-target training pairs. In contrast, pairwise-based methods overlook the global topological structure, which is essential for comprehensively capturing regulatory mechanisms. Results: To address these limitations, we propose scGPL, an end-to-end unified framework that jointly models global regulatory topology and local interactions. scGPL extracts macro-level features from the global regulatory graph and introduces a dynamic, importance-guided subgraph sampling mechanism to capture fine-grained local dependencies. By fusing global representations with subgraph-enhanced local features, our framework bridges the gap between the two paradigms, incorporating essential whole-graph topological dependencies while retaining the data abundance advantage of pairwise methods. Extensive experiments on seven benchmark datasets demonstrate that scGPL consistently achieves state-of-the-art performance, with up to 13.7% improvement over the strongest baseline, validating the effectiveness of our integrative design. Availability and implementation: The source code is maintained on GitHub (https://github.com/talent-hang/scGPL), and the datasets and versioned releases are archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21608485 for reproducibility.
evidence_items.title: Bridging Graph and Pairwise Learning for Gene Regulatory Network Inference from scRNA-seq Data

evidence_items.summary: Selecting an LLM for next-step recommendation requires benchmarks that reflect the intended educational task and domain. We present a benchmarking method that uses Knowledge Space Theory (KST) as a formal evaluation reference. Given a task catalogue and an existing prerequisite relation, the method derives admissible knowledge states and the complete set of immediate next steps for each state. Recommendations generated by a model under a specified prompt are compared with these reference sets. A sample evaluation study uses 2,400 responses from six models across four mathematics domains, four prompt conditions, and two catalogue orders. Exact-set accuracy was 61.3% with descriptions only, 62.8% when models were asked to reconstruct prerequisites, 96.3% with supplied prerequisite relations, and 98.2% with the complete knowledge space. Performance varied across models and domains, and recommendation sets agreed across the two presentations in 85.25% of pairs. The benchmark supports comparisons of model-prompt combinations against a context-specific reference. Its scores describe structural recommendation accuracy under the evaluated conditions; they do not establish learning benefit or the necessity of using an LLM for selection.
evidence_items.title: Benchmarking LLM Next-Step Recommendations with Knowledge Space Theory

evidence_items.summary: Low-bit quantization reduces the inference cost of LLM agents but can compromise task success. Examining failed rollouts, we find that quantized agents overlook task requirements or environmental conditions, producing environment transitions that diverge from successful full-precision references. Correcting these behavioral divergences remains difficult: offline data may miss the student's failure contexts, while its own rollouts may provide few correct responses in those contexts. We introduce SteerDistill, a quantization-aware distillation method in which a full-precision teacher guides the student to revise failed responses and iteratively refines its guidance using feedback from student execution. This closed-loop teacher steering produces locally verified behavioral corrections. We internalize these corrections by training the student without guidance to match the steered student's predictions at corrected turns and the full-precision teacher's at other turns, enabling unassisted inference. Across five agentic benchmarks and three models, SteerDistill exceeds the strongest quantized baseline by 1.67--2.18 points in average score under W4A16 and stays within one point of BF16. On $\tau^2$-Bench, it outperforms QeRL by 1.84 percentage points in success rate using 67% fewer training GPU hours and produces shorter successful trajectories than the quantized baselines.
evidence_items.title: SteerDistill: Quantizing LLM Agents via Closed-Loop Teacher Steering

evidence_items.summary: Organizations use engineers' token spend to monitor AI adoption, set budgets, and measure productivity, but the metric's relationship with engineering output is unclear. We link five weeks of token usage in coding agents to the commits of 404 engineers at JetBrains, and analyze a company survey of 412 employees. We find that token spend varied mostly between engineers, and which engineers spent the most stayed largely the same over the five weeks. Among weeks with similar commit counts, the 90th percentile of spend was 39 to 240 times the 10th. Within an engineer, doubling spend was associated with about 10% more commits. Available work metrics explained 38% of the variation in spend between engineers and 13% of the week-to-week variation within an engineer. In the survey, respondents in technical roles reported in nearly nine of ten agent evaluations using agents for tasks beyond coding, such as analysis, research, and planning. Token spend therefore measures how much engineers use agents across many kinds of work and not the outcome and value of that work. We recommend using token spend at most for resource accounting, and evaluating agent-assisted work with evidence about tasks and outcomes.
evidence_items.title: The AI Era's Lines of Code? A Case Study on What an Engineer's Token Spend Measures

evidence_items.summary: Fine-tuning large-scale foundation models across resource-constrained, distributed clients presents significant computational and communication challenges. While merging Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) with Federated Learning (FL) enables rank-based flexibility, the interdependence of the adaptation matrices ($\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$) often complicates optimization. In this work, we theoretically demonstrate that LoRA fine-tuning with Gaussian initialization and a frozen $\mathbf{A}$ matrix acts as a stochastic approximation of full fine-tuning, where batch gradients are subject to a random, rank-dependent perturbation. Motivated by this insight, we propose freezing and periodically resampling $\mathbf{A}$ matrices at the client level. This strategy decouples the $\mathbf{A}$ and $\mathbf{B}$ gradients, diminishes LoRA low-rank constraints and reduces both computational and uplink communication overheads by 50\%, allowing for the reallocation of resources toward higher adaptation ranks. Furthermore, we show that in this frozen-$\mathbf{A}$ regime, the adaptation rank $r$ directly governs the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of the perturbed gradients. Specifically, we find that the SNR increases linearly with $r$, implying that clients' learning rates must be dynamically scaled with their adaptation ranks for higher utility. Building on these foundations, we introduce SPRA-LoRA (Stochastic Projection Rank-Aware LoRA), a federated rank-aware fine-tuning strategy that utilizes frozen, resampled $\mathbf{A}$ matrices and rank-dependent learning rates for clients. We also prove its convergence with heterogeneous client resources. Our experiments across benchmark datasets demonstrate that SPRA-LoRA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines with half the overhead on clients.
evidence_items.title: Stochastic Projections and Rank-Aware Learning Rates for Federated LoRA

evidence_items.summary: Temporal Sentence Grounding (TSG) aims to localize temporal segments in untrimmed videos that correspond to natural language queries, a critical task for video understanding with applications in video retrieval, summarization, and human-computer interaction. Despite significant progress driven by transformer-based models, existing TSG methods suffer from two key limitations: quantization errors due to temporal downsampling, which misalign segment boundaries, and suboptimal ranking of predictions based on semantic matching rather than localization precision. To address these challenges, we propose the Adaptive Boundary Refinement and Ranking (ABRR) framework, a novel, model-agnostic post-processing approach that enhances the performance of any TSG model without retraining. ABRR integrates three innovative components: (1) Temporal Distribution Smoothing, which mitigates noise in predicted score distributions using Gaussian kernel convolution; (2) Boundary Refinement via Optimal Transport, which leverages the 2-Wasserstein distance and Sinkhorn iterations to align coarse segment boundaries with true temporal moments, grounded in Monge-Kantorovich optimal transport theory; and (3) Quality-Driven Re-Ranking, which reorders predictions using a composite score balancing localization precision and semantic relevance. By correcting quantization errors and prioritizing accurately localized segments, ABRR achieves substantial improvements over state-of-the-art TSG models. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets, including Charades-STA, ActivityNet Captions, and QVHighlights, demonstrate consistent gains at stringent IoU thresholds (e.g., IoU=0.7), alongside enhanced ranking performance. The framework's computational efficiency and compatibility with existing models make it a versatile and impactful solution for real-world TSG applications.
evidence_items.title: ABRR: Transforming Temporal Sentence Grounding with Wasserstein-Adaptive Refinement and Precision Ranking

evidence_items.summary: Children's earliest years are a period of intense social learning, during which meaning is built through gaze, gesture, and physical contact. Yet, this critical aspect of social interaction remains under-evaluated in multimodal video understanding, as existing benchmarks prioritize the conversation-driven interactions of adults. We address this gap with \bench ($\textbf{N}$aturalistic $\textbf{E}$arly-childhood $\textbf{S}$ocial in$\textbf{T}$eractions), the first child-centric benchmark for nonverbal social reasoning. \bench comprises \totalvids manually annotated clips ($\sim$12s) curated for diversity across naturalistic settings, cultural contexts, and developmental stages. Beyond a lack of data, targeted model improvement in this domain is hindered by coarse evaluation schemas that conflate basic perception with higher-order reasoning. To resolve this, \bench introduces a compositional schema that builds atomic interaction cues into progressive levels of social reasoning: contextual, behavioral, interpersonal, and open-ended descriptions. Extensive analysis of state-of-the-art Vision-Language Models (VLMs) reveals a stark performance collapse: despite strong contextual recognition, models exhibit substantial gaps in decoding precise behavioral and interpersonal cues. We trace these failures to specific biases, including poor consequence grounding and temporal sensitivity. Finally, we ground \bench in real-world applications by evaluating VLMs using domain adaptation strategies. Ultimately, \bench provides a rigorous testbed for advancing socially grounded artificial intelligence in early childhood. Project page: https://laubravo.github.io/nest_website/.
evidence_items.title: Before Words, Beyond Speech: Evaluating Nonverbal Social Reasoning in Early Childhood

evidence_items.summary: Accurate and timely identification of road closures is critical for large-scale navigation and logistics systems, yet remains challenging due to the need to jointly reason over visual evidence, spatial context, and road network topology. Existing approaches either rely on manual map updates or focus on detecting closure-related objects without resolving which road segment is affected. In this work, we introduce a unified multimodal and multitask framework that jointly performs road closure classification (no, partial, complete) and road segment association within a single learning architecture. Our model integrates graph-structured map data, satellite imagery augmented with projected street-level detections, and street-view images using modality-specific encoders and cross-modal transformer attention, enabling explicit reasoning over visual cues and network topology. Evaluated on nearly 20K real-world scenarios collected from a large-scale commercial vehicle fleet, our approach achieves 72.7% closure classification accuracy and 60% road segment association accuracy, outperforming frontier vision-language models by over 28 percentage points on closure classification while being over 4,000x smaller and 100x faster at inference. Extensive ablations demonstrate the importance of cross-modal attention, edge-aware pooling, and graph message passing for accurate geospatial reasoning. This work establishes the first benchmark for joint road closure classification and segment-level attribution, and shows that task-specific architectural inductive biases substantially outperform general-purpose multimodal models for structured geospatial understanding.
evidence_items.title: Multimodal Road Closure Mapping via Cross-Modal Graph Attention

evidence_items.summary: Graphical user interface (GUI) grounding maps a screenshot and a natural-language instruction to the screen location where an agent should act. Zoomed views can reveal small targets but may lose the context needed to identify them. We introduce GroundCascade, a training-free controller that uses agreement between a grounder's full-screen and zoomed predictions to decide when to consult a complementary model. It selects between zoomed predictions while preserving corroborated full-screen locations. An optional Finalizer predicts from an unmarked joint crop when disagreement remains (Full); omitting it yields the two-stage Selective variant. GroundCascade reaches 85.33% on ScreenSpot-Pro with Indeed-UI-32B/8B/32B and 88.43% on the visible-target OSWorld-G-Refined subset with Qwen3.6-27B/3.8-27B/3.8-27B, gains of 2.66 and 2.35 percentage points over the stronger standalone two-pass grounder. On UI-Vision, GroundCascade reaches 72.20% category-balanced accuracy, with Selective slightly higher at 72.28%. Across these three evaluations, GroundCascade in Full mode uses 2.42-2.73 calls per request, 31-39% fewer than unconditionally acquiring both models' two-pass predictions. At matched second-model call budgets, selective acquisition gains 1.52-2.56 points over standalone Two-pass, compared with 0.22-0.69 points from stratified random acquisition. GroundCascade leads the official ScreenSpot-Pro leaderboard and exceeds reported GUI-specialist comparisons on OSWorld-G-Refined and UI-Vision, subject to differences in external evaluation protocols.
evidence_items.title: GroundCascade: Selective Second Opinions for GUI Grounding

evidence_items.summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are typically evaluated by whether they produce correct answers, but correctness alone does not reveal whether their outputs are supported by the right visual evidence. We introduce VIGOR, a benchmark for evaluating VIsually GrOunded Rationales in MLLMs. VIGOR represents visual rationales as explicit concepts paired with pixel-level groundings, covering multiple abstraction levels including low-level visual properties, intermediate structures, objects, parts and high-level motion, relations. To construct VIGOR at scale, we develop an automatic annotation framework that reuses existing dense supervision when available and generates missing concept groundings through proposal-based annotation followed by conservative multimodal verification. Using VIGOR, we evaluate whether MLLMs "look at what they say" by comparing model-derived visual evidence for each expressed concept against annotated ground-truth rationales. Our results show that current MLLMs exhibit limited visual rationale correctness and reveal distinct grounding failures across concept levels. VIGOR provides a benchmark and scalable data construction pipeline for studying whether MLLM outputs are supported by appropriate visual evidence. Code is available at https://github.com/deep-real/VIGOR
evidence_items.title: VIGOR: Benchmarking Visual Rationale Correctness in Multimodal Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Knowledge editing has emerged as a promising approach for efficiently updating embedded knowledge in large language models (LLMs). It first computes an ideal target hidden state that steers the LLM toward the new output, and then edits the model parameters so that the original hidden state is mapped to this target. While most existing methods focus on the second stage of parameter editing in preserving other knowledge, we find that the upstream construction of the target hidden state also plays an important role in allocating the model's limited capacity space. We first establish a theoretical connection between interference in the parameter space and interference between target hidden states, showing that the two are positively correlated. Building on this insight, we propose a simple yet effective $\ell_1$ regularization method that prunes away unnecessary ``tentacles'' of each knowledge vector, retaining only the essential components. With fewer extraneous tentacles, each edit affects less other knowledge, enabling better coexistence. Extensive experiments across multiple LLMs and benchmark datasets verify the effectiveness of our method. Code: https://github.com/wintersdragon-c/STO.
evidence_items.title: Capacity Allocation at the Source: Sparse Target Optimization for LLM Knowledge Editing

evidence_items.summary: This work presents a new benchmark that aims to address the limitations of current methods for evaluating LLMs in Brazilian Portuguese. We introduced Brasilidade, an assessment methodology comprised of standardized tasks distributed across four different domains, and we are making available the tasks from its first domain, which address nuances of the language, grammar, and variations of Brazilian Portuguese. The results show that model size, by itself, does not determine performance; several medium-sized models outperformed larger models in the protocols evaluated. Specific models for Portuguese, in general, did not perform above average, despite their targeted training. Different task levels revealed significant nuances: while some tasks proved easy for most models, others posed extreme challenges, and some yielded mixed results, with wide variations in performance. This clearly illustrates the need for benchmarks that address the limitations of the models in Brazilian Portuguese, allowing future training cycles to seek to overcome them. Project repository https://github.com/soberania-oficial/brasilidade
evidence_items.title: Brasilidade: Measuring Brazilian Identity for Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: When should a robot look at the cup, and when at the portafilter? A view that is informative for one task can be useless for another, even at the same workstation. We introduce Seeing What Execution Needs, a benchmark for task-conditioned actionable spatial belief in simulated tabletop manipulation. Its aligned three-domain track contains 1,080 frozen cases (360 each for coffee workstation, drawer/cabinet, and microwave/appliance). The primary coffee protocols -- closed-loop actionability and same-object functional out-of-distribution generalization -- produce over 115,000 evaluator episodes across evaluated methods, budgets, and inference repeats. Each case pairs candidate RGB views with a manipulation command, shared scripted skills, and hidden postconditions, directly measuring whether selected observations support execution. A metadata-assisted diagnostic reference pipeline maintains spatial-functional beliefs and ranks views by missing evidence. At primary budget settings, it reaches 98.8% closed-loop and 98.9% functional-OOD success; removing functional fields or command binding reduces functional-OOD success to 0.0% and 19.7%, respectively. Under a separate full-preview contract, seven vision-language models reach 26-43%. Replacing coverage metadata with frozen RGB-derived scores retains 98.5%/98.9% success; shuffling these scores reduces success to 15%/11%, supporting dependence on image content. Separately, the aligned three-domain evaluation at H=3 supports portability of the benchmark interface under frozen domain-specific schemas. These results suggest that spatial belief for manipulation should be evaluated by whether acquired evidence meets the current command's execution requirements.
evidence_items.title: Seeing What Execution Needs: Benchmarking Task-Conditioned Actionable Spatial Belief for Manipulation

evidence_items.summary: Federated Learning (FL) enables distributed clients to jointly train a global model without sharing their raw data. However, deploying the resulting deep neural networks on resource-constrained edge devices remains challenging due to their inference-time computational and memory requirements. Binary Neural Networks (BNNs) offer substantial efficiency gains by representing weights and activations using a single bit, but achieving competitive accuracy under such aggressive quantization remains difficult. Rotation-aware binarization reduces quantization errors by aligning real-valued weights with their binary representations. Despite its effectiveness in centralized learning, applying rotation-aware binarization in FL is non-trivial due to discrepancies between local and global models, particularly under heterogeneous client data distributions. To address this challenge, we propose FedBNN, a federated rotation-aware binarization framework that leverages global model information to guide local binarization while incorporating locally learned rotation information into server-side construction of the global binary model. Experiments across multiple benchmark datasets, model architectures, and degrees of data heterogeneity demonstrate that the proposed integrated methodology achieves accuracy competitive with full-precision federated models while generally outperforming existing federated binary learning approaches. Overall, FedBNN enables accurate binary inference in heterogeneous federated settings, with savings of up to $58\times$ in FLOPs and $32\times$ in memory over full-precision models, offering a practical balance between predictive performance and deployment efficiency on resource-constrained edge devices.
evidence_items.title: Federated Learning of Binary Neural Networks: Enabling Low-Cost Inference

evidence_items.summary: Volumetric computed tomography (CT) segmentation supports quantitative image analysis, but most AI-based methods remain organ-specific, with fragmented models, inconsistent label definitions, and heterogeneous training and evaluation protocols. Here we present CADS, a unified data-model framework for scalable and generalizable whole-body CT segmentation. We construct a SNOMED-CT-referenced anatomical label space harmonizing heterogeneous cohorts from over 100 imaging centers, yielding complete annotations of 167 structures across 22,022 CT volumes and markedly expanding anatomical coverage and scale beyond existing resources. To complete labels on sparsely annotated CTs, we combine self-training with shape-informed quality control based on neural implicit functions, curating high-quality pseudo-labels. Trained on this resource, CADS shows robust whole-body segmentation across distribution shifts and improved performance relative to state-of-the-art approaches across 18 public datasets. We further validate it in an independent, expert-reviewed real-world oncology cohort of 2,864 CTs. The curated dataset, pretrained models, and user-friendly software together provide an accessible, reproducible foundation for large-scale anatomical segmentation and computational anatomy research.
evidence_items.title: CADS: A Comprehensive Anatomical Dataset and Segmentation for Whole-Body Anatomy in Computed Tomography

Key Features & Upgrades in Version 1.3.0:1. Complete Radiative Transfer Coupling & 330 Archived MODTRAN 5.2 Decks: All simulated radiances strictly satisfy the full surface-leaving boundary condition L surf = epsilon B(T s) + (1 - epsilon) L down and Top-of-Atmosphere coupling L TOA = tau L surf + L up across 30 distinct MODTRAN 5.2 profiles (6 standard atmospheric models x 5 water vapor scaling factors, PWV from 0.21 to 6.77 g/cm²), shipped alongside all 330 executed MODTRAN input decks.2. Operational Atmospheric-Correction Error Propagation (N4) & Sensor Noise: Network inputs are derived through operational atmospheric correction using estimated atmospheres perturbed by realistic precipitable water vapor (PWV) retrieval errors and sensor-specific NEΔT detector noise (0.3 K for ASTER, 0.2 K for HyTES).3. evidence_items.summary: Accurate modelling of illumination is central to realistic image synthesis and scene understanding. Yet, there is little exploration into whether image generative models are good at this task or whether physical plausibility remains a key challenge for them. Clearly, significant progress has been made in realistic image synthesis, but do models truly understand lighting in a physically accurate manner? To answer this question, this work proposes a benchmark to assess the lighting understanding and harmonisation capabilities of generative models. Our key insight is that evaluating lighting understanding for such models only requires testing how well they insert novel objects into real photographs whilst maintaining consistent illumination. To do so, we use a multi-illumination dataset with images containing simple objects serving as "light probes", and prompt models to inpaint the same object onto the original image, then compare the generated results against the ground-truth light probes. We then estimate the lighting direction, colour and radiance distribution from the inpainted probes, providing a quantitative measure of illumination accuracy and photometric realism. Our work establishes a scalable evaluation protocol to systematically assess how well generative models capture and reproduce real-world lighting, offering a foundation for benchmarking the photometric accuracy of any future models. All code and data are available at https://lvsn.github.io/SheddingLight/.
evidence_items.title: Shedding Light: A Benchmark for Evaluating Lighting Understanding in Generative Image Models

evidence_items.summary: BERT has become one of the most effective Natural Language Processing (NLP) models for sentiment analysis due to its ability to generate contextual representations. However, previous studies have reported that BERT often exhibits imbalanced precision, recall, and F1-score across sentiment classes when trained on imbalanced datasets. This study investigates the effectiveness of data augmentation in improving the performance of two pretrained language models, IndoBERT and IndoBERTweet, on a TAPERA policy dataset containing 3,364 preprocessed tweets and a benchmark dataset with 12,693 instances. Data augmentation was applied only to the training data using Synonym Replacement (15%, 25%, and 35%), Back Translation, Masked Language Modeling (15%, 25%, and 35%), and Masked Language Modeling combined with Cosine Similarity. Model performance was evaluated using Accuracy and Macro F1-score. The best performance on the TAPERA dataset was achieved by IndoBERTweet with Masked Language Modeling (25%), yielding a Macro F1-score of 0.8421 and an Accuracy of 0.8880. On the benchmark dataset, IndoBERTweet with Synonym Replacement (25%) achieved the highest Macro F1-score (0.9346) and Accuracy (0.9520). These findings provide a comparative evaluation of augmentation strategies for IndoBERT-based sentiment analysis and offer practical guidance for handling class imbalance across different datasets.
evidence_items.title: Optimizing Indobert for Imbalanced  Sentiment Analysis Using Data Augmentation on Tapera and Benchmark Datasets

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Integrating heterogeneous repositories into a single knowledge base, and completing each source’s missing attributes by supervised imputation, is routine in data engineering, but its effect on downstream evaluation is rarely measured. We study it in cyber-attack forecasting, where individual incident repositories are either temporally dated or categorically shallow. To our knowledge, the resulting form of leakage has not been described for merged threat-intelligence corpora. Harmonising the VERIS Community Database with Hackmageddon timelines into 20,279 incidents under a common 64-attribute schema, we find attack-type macro F1 of 70.41% on records whose labels were reconstructed during merging against 26.58% on records whose labels were observed, a 43.83-point gap (p < 0.0001) that pooled metrics conceal. Because the sources cover disjoint periods, a masked-imputation control holding era and source constant isolates the effect: inflation persists at 16.86 points (p = 0.012) and scales inversely with imputer fidelity, so a weak imputation step distorts evaluation more than a strong one. We propose a source-agnostic, three-part protocol (provenance stratification, feature-group ablation and the masked-imputation control) applicable to any integrated dataset. Entity embeddings raise attack-type macro F1 from 14.00% to 32.57% at fixed architecture, and class cardinality rather than imbalance bounds performance: the 189-class country target reaches at most 7.32% macro F1 despite 66.79% accuracy. Under chronological evaluation, attack-type forecasting reaches 38.44% accuracy and 19.32% macro F1, and the deep model overtakes the tree-based baseline (p < 0.003). Code, taxonomy and corpus-construction scripts are released.
evidence_items.title: Entity Embeddings and Ensemble Learning for Multi-Attribute Cyber-Attack Forecasting: A Benchmark and Evaluation Protocol for Merged Incident Repositories

evidence_items.summary: Abstract We present Evalita-LLM, a novel benchmark designed to evaluate Large Language Models (LLMs) on Italian tasks. The key innovation of Evalita-LLM is the use of multiple prompts for each task, which mitigates the model’s sensitivity to specific prompt formulations and ensures a robust and objective performance assessment. We propose an iterative methodology for selecting and validating multiple prompts, and metrics that capture both high performance and stability of a prompt given a set of LLMs. The resulting Evalita-LLM multi-prompt benchmark is based on ten native Italian tasks, eliminating translation issues and potential cultural biases. It includes a mix of multiple-choice and generative tasks, enabling more natural interactions with LLMs. We report experimental results from the benchmark’s development phase, along with performance statistics for several state-of-the-art LLMs. Evalita-LLM is publicly available with a leaderboard hosted on Hugging Face to support transparent evaluation and comparison of LLMs.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating LLMs on Italian through multi-prompt: the Evalita-LLM benchmark

evidence_items.summary: V2G-MAAC is a semi-synthetic benchmark dataset for multi-authority access control in vehicle-to-grid (V2G) charging networks. It is built on real EV charging-session structure from ACN-Data (Lee, Li & Low, 2019) and extends it with three independently injected, ground-truth threat axes spanning the three authorities present in a V2G session — the Charge Point Operator (CPO), the e-Mobility Service Provider (eMSP), and the Electric Vehicle (EV) itself — plus a fourth, parallel identity-delegation axis (acting identity vs. home identity for each authority). The release contains seven variants sharing one generator configuration: a reference configuration (main), three independent reseeds (seed 101, seed 103, seed 104) for distinguishing genuine reproducibility from variant-induced change, and three stress conditions (adversarial: threat-layer parameters shift over time; noisy benign: elevated behavioral noise among honest actors; sparse feedback: reduced availability of running, history-dependent features). Each variant contains 125,110 charging sessions (108,060 train / 17,050 test), with a day-blocked temporal split reconstructable from the included split column. Each session carries billing/latency/energy-rate deviation features, charge-session timing, an actor’s own flagged-session history, EV session-reuse share, and certificate-validity/roaming/peak-hour context flags, alongside per-axis binary ground truth (gt cpo malicious, gt emsp malicious, gt ev sybil — the first two onset-gated) and pooled convenience labels (risk factor count, composite risk score). A fourth, parallel identity-delegation axis (gt cpo delegate malicious, gt emsp delegate malicious, gt ev delegate abuse) is reported as an exploratory finding, not a fully evaluated baseline-ladder rung.
evidence_items.title: V2G-MAAC: A Semi-Synthetic Benchmark Dataset for Multi-Authority Access Control in Vehicle-to-Grid Charging Networks

To address this limitation, we construct GeoKnowQA. We first integrate existing geography classification systems to establish a multi-level disciplinary taxonomy that defines the target knowledge scope. We then systematically collect textbooks and professional monographs for individual subfields, and construct training and evaluation data through automated generation, quality filtering, and manual review. evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and autonomous agents are creating new opportunities for hardware design optimization. This paper examines three connected directions toward autonomous RTL and synthesis optimization: (1) Realistic benchmarking. We discuss reference-based and open-ended RTL optimization benchmarks that evaluate optimization opportunities under realistic EDA workflows. (2) Tool-grounded RTL optimization. We present Dr. RTL, a multi-agent framework that automates critical-path analysis, RTL rewriting, and implementation-level evaluation, while continuously improving through reusable optimization skills. Evaluated on 20 real-world RTL designs, Dr.~RTL achieves average WNS/TNS improvements of 21\%/17\% with a 6\% area reduction over commercial synthesis. (3) Design-specific synthesis optimization. We explore agent-driven synthesis script tuning and the discovery of executable synthesis algorithms across intermediate representations, technology-independent optimization, and technology mapping. Finally, we envision AI-native design automation that jointly explores architectural, RTL, and EDA algorithm design spaces, guided by verification constraints and implementation feedback.
evidence_items.title: Toward Autonomous RTL and Synthesis Optimization: Benchmarking and Self-Improving Agents

evidence_items.summary: BACKGROUND: AI-based tools are expected to play a key role in lung cancer screening (LCS). The evaluation of these tools often relied on private datasets or fragmented public datasets with inconsistent availability of clinical data and expert nodule annotations. This has hindered reproducibility, comparability, and independent assessment of AI tools. To address these gaps, we present LUCQUE, a novel, large, comprehensively annotated dataset derived from LDCT lung cancer screening in Québec, which is accessible for reliable AI evaluation. METHODS: LUCQUE was curated and is hosted on PARADIM, a digital infrastructure supporting DICOM data de-identification, annotation, long-term storage and analysis. LDCT scans and clinical information were combined to a curated collection and complemented by voxel-level, expert-derived pulmonary nodule and cyst segmentations, and Lung-RADS-based lesion characteristics. Key dataset characteristics and statistics were reported, including participant demographics, imaging parameters, radiological findings, and segmented lesion characteristics. Dataset analyses were conducted according to PARADIM's model-to-data approach, in which user code is executed on the platform such that data remains on premise. RESULTS: LUCQUE currently comprises 1,678 LDCT baseline studies from 1,678 participants. Most studies were classified as Lung-RADS 2. A total of 1,776 pulmonary nodules and 60 cysts were annotated, with a median (interquartile range) volume of $89\,(56,\,159)\,\mathrm{mm}^3$ and $1,384\,(589,\,3793)\,\mathrm{mm}^3$ respectively. CONCLUSIONS: Compared to publicly available LCS datasets, LUCQUE currently represents the largest accessible annotated real-world LCS dataset. Access to LUCQUE is provided via a model-to-data approach, enabling privacy-preserving, reproducible, and independent real-world evaluation of AI tools in LCS.
evidence_items.title: LUCQUE: A lung cancer screening dataset from Québec for reliable AI evaluation

evidence_items.summary: The design of manufacturing systems relies on discrete-event simulation (DES) models that experts still build in tool-specific interfaces. AI agents can now write simulation code, but every model they write from scratch is new, unverified software. We present SimuLean, an open-source 3D DES simulator on the Unity engine designed to be programmed by AI agents: its modelling semantics are verified once, in the platform, and the agent builds and studies one model through domain-level commands, in the 3D scene or headless; physically simulated durations are calibrated for fast headless studies. We evaluated it on 18 manufacturing modelling tasks, from single machines to published production lines. A frontier agent built valid models in 93 of 108 attempts (86%), in about two minutes each; on the benchmark's interface version, two frontier agents built 105 of 108 models through domain commands alone, so that each comes with a record of how it was built. Every residual failure was silent - a model that builds and runs but answers wrongly - and only comparison with reference models revealed them all. In an industrial case, one agent working alone rebuilt, verified and studied a robotised welding workshop from a published study, in SimuLean and in SimPy. Comparing them with the published, expert-built model exposed an error in it; against the corrected model, the agent-built models agree within 1%. One agent can already build complete, realistic and traceable models for the design of manufacturing systems; independent reference models are what make them trustworthy.
evidence_items.title: Agentic discrete-event simulation for manufacturing system design: an open 3D simulator, a benchmark and an industrial case

evidence_items.summary: Clinical large language model agents depend on both model capability and the surrounding system that selects information, constrains actions, and verifies execution. In this Viewpoint, we argue that this harness should be an explicit unit of clinical agent design, evaluation, and reporting. Our aim is to help clinical informatics and development teams specify this layer and to help evaluators and institutional governance teams assess its contributions and risks. Selected benchmarks show substantial performance differences across harness configurations, but architecture comparisons, bundled improvements, and within-model component comparisons support different levels of causal attribution. We propose a revisable 3-tier framework: tier 1 specifies general orchestration functions, including prompts, tools, output schemas, control flow, memory, and generic verification; tier 2 specifies their clinical adaptations for knowledge integration, differential reasoning, missingness and temporality, safety verification, and workflow alignment; and tier 3 specifies a failure-driven evaluation cycle applied to both. Our contribution is a framework that makes these connections explicit. We provide classification rules, an illustrative clinical example, a proposed evaluation protocol, and a minimum reporting checklist. Observable execution traces are distinguished from private model reasoning, with provenance and privacy safeguards supporting retrospective reconstruction. Evaluation should separate task success, clinical correctness, process safety, and operational reliability. Lightweight fine-tuning can complement harness design; their interaction requires controlled study. The framework is a proposal for empirical testing, not a validated taxonomy or evidence of deployment safety.
evidence_items.title: Beyond Model Choice: A Harness-Centered Framework for Designing Clinical Large Language Model Agents

evidence_items.summary: Background Synthetic population and persona datasets can provide artificial individual-level records without exposing personal data. However, for surveillance use, they must preserve the joint profiles that define vulnerable groups, not only marginal distributions. Objective This study evaluated whether a public statistics–based Korean synthetic persona dataset is consistent with Korea Community Health Survey (CHS) and Korean Statistical Information Service (KOSIS) benchmarks for auxiliary small-area public health surveillance. Methods We compared 1,000,000 synthetic persona rows with 1,156,122 adult respondents from the 2021-2025 CHS and selected KOSIS municipal indicators. Core variables were age group, sex, marital status, living-alone status, and education; province or municipal area replaced marital status in the regional profiles. Economic activity and occupation were treated as sensitivity domains. We compared marginal and joint distributions using percentage-point differences and total variation distance (TVD) and quantified CHS sampling uncertainty using 500-replicate stratified cluster percentile bootstrap intervals and compared high-dimensional TVD with CHS split-half references. Sparse-cell, KOSIS correlation, and regional composition-standardized analyses assessed robustness and potential downstream use. Results Persona rows were close to CHS for sex (TVD<0.001, 95% bootstrap percentile interval 0.000-0.001), province (TVD 0.006, bootstrap percentile interval 0.005-0.006), living-alone status (TVD 0.008, bootstrap percentile interval 0.007-0.009), and age group (TVD 0.013, bootstrap percentile interval 0.012-0.014). Differences were larger for marital status (TVD 0.039, bootstrap percentile interval 0.038-0.040) and education (TVD 0.059, bootstrap percentile interval 0.058-0.061).
evidence_items.title: Viability of Public Statistics–Based Synthetic Personas in Small-Area Public Health Surveillance: Sociodemographic Benchmark Consistency Study Using Korea Community Health Survey and Korean Statistical Information Service Data

evidence_items.summary: Computational chemistry, increasingly enabled by high-performance computing, accelerates research across many areas of chemistry. However, heterogeneous software packages, input formats, and output conventions create a steep learning curve that also complicates simulation scripting and automation. Large language models (LLMs) can lower this barrier by helping users prepare calculations, execute workflows, and interpret results. We present ASSAY (Agentic Simulation Suite for Automated Chemistry), an open-source agentic toolkit for quantum chemistry designed for undergraduate CC education. To align ASSAY with current curricula, we analyzed syllabi from 17 courses at public and private universities in and outside the United States. ASSAY supports example-driven learning through input generation and output interpretation, while its local and remote workflows can introduce students to distributed computing, batch queues, and file management. In a benchmark spanning 12 skills and 8 LLMs, ASSAY achieved a mean pass rate of 94.04%, with six models achieving at least 98%. These results establish ASSAY as a reproducible, integrity-first foundation for making computational chemistry more accessible to students and reliable for researchers.
evidence_items.title: Development and Evaluation of an Agentic Suite of Tasks Covering a Computational Chemistry Curriculum

organizations: Tay Bac University
evidence_items.summary: Abstract The Minimum s-Club Cover (MSCC) problem is an NP-hard and APX-hard combinatorial optimization challenge on graphs with significant applications in social network community detection, computational molecular biology, and telecommunication routing. Despite its theoretical and operational relevance, computational research on MSCC currently suffers from a lack of standardized open benchmark instances, absence of granular per-run execution logs, and inconsistent feasibility reporting. To bridge these critical methodological gaps and promote open science, this paper presents a comprehensive, standardized, and fully reproducible empirical benchmark suite for MSCC ($s=2$). The dataset encompasses 30 standardized benchmark graph instances partitioned into two distinct structural families: 12 real-world complex networks from biological, social, and information domains, and 18 symmetric DIMACS benchmark graphs with varying topological densities. Across these 30 instances, we provide 4,800 complete optimization runs conducted over 20 synchronized paired random seeds and eight comparative algorithms spanning constructive heuristics, static/random evolutionary algorithms, and adaptive learning-augmented baselines. All discovered solutions are strictly verified through breadth-first search and all-pairs shortest path calculations, achieving a verified 100% feasibility rate. We report granular raw logs, aggregated summary metrics, optimal random seed distributions, and non-parametric Wilcoxon signed-rank tests with Holm-Bonferroni correction ($1-\beta > 0.85$). All graph instances, raw/aggregated data, configuration files, and verification scripts are released openly under the permissive Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International license.
evidence_items.title: A Reproducible Benchmark Dataset and Experimental Evaluation for the Minimum s-Club Cover Problem

evidence_items.summary: Existing evaluations often test persona expression rather than whether persona information persists in extended decision-making. We introduce THEATRON, a controlled benchmark that uses financial replay to evaluate persona persistence in long-horizon sequential decision-making. In these environments, models conditioned on fixed behavioral-finance personas observe shared daily market evidence and trajectory-specific account-state feedback and make sequential decisions over multi-month trajectories. We evaluate Zero-Shot, One-Shot, and Chain-of-Thought persona injection across four LLMs, using cumulative-return and action trajectories to diagnose within-persona stability, cross-persona separability, and action collapse. Persona conditioning produces systematic behavioral shifts beyond a no-persona baseline, and persona-level separation generally exceeds the variation induced by semantically equivalent descriptions. Nevertheless, these shifts do not reliably form coherent persona-specific policies: apparently stable separation can arise from stereotyped action collapse, while diverse policies can exhibit noisy trajectory switching. These findings expose a gap between observable persona-induced behavior and persistent, context-sensitive persona-conditioned decision policies. Code and benchmark data are publicly available at: https://github.com/yuyan12138/theatron
evidence_items.title: THEATRON: A Benchmark for Evaluating Persona Persistence in Long-Horizon LLM Decision-Making

evidence_items.summary: This paper contains examples of stereotypes about veterans and displaced people that may be offensive or distressing. Social bias benchmarks for language models commonly examine categories such as gender, race, and religion, often drawn from lists of legally protected characteristics. Veterans and internally displaced people (IDPs) fall outside these lists, and stereotypes about them, which can undermine access to employment, housing, and social participation, remain largely absent from language model evaluation. We introduce WarBias, a Ukrainian-English benchmark of stereotypes about these two groups. Built from a taxonomy of 120 stereotype claims grounded in research and monitoring reports, WarBias contains 1,007 stereotype-counter-stereotype-unrelated sentence triplets and 240 multiple-choice questions per language. A Ukrainian language model selected in a blinded human pilot generated the Ukrainian triplets. At least two independent annotators reviewed each triplet in the annotation cohort. The authors revised items in response to the reviews, and the final release was machine-translated into English. Each claim carries a human severity rating. In a baseline evaluation of six models, four prefer stereotypical Ukrainian sentences about at least one group, most strongly about IDPs, while English scores are mostly balanced. WarBias supports complementary evaluations of stereotypical preferences and context-sensitive judgments, and provides paired forget/retain material for unlearning-based bias mitigation. We document the benchmark's construction, intended uses, and limitations, and offer its construction method as a template for analogous benchmarks in other conflict-affected societies.
evidence_items.title: WarBias: A Bilingual LLM Benchmark of Stereotypes About Internally Displaced People and Veterans

evidence_items.summary: LLMs can now draft complete multi-episode dramas, and LLM judges are increasingly used to evaluate them. Assessing the reliability of these judges is difficult because drama quality encompasses specification-backed errors, reproducible preferences, and legitimate disagreement among human raters. Most existing evaluations reduce these cases to a single score from one judge call and leave tie calibration, call-to-call variation, and the vote margin underlying the human reference unreported. We introduce DramaGrow, a regime-aware benchmark and audit protocol for AI-generated Chinese five-episode drama. The benchmark assigns verifiable constraint violations, four-of-five preferences, and within-panel disagreements to separate denominators and evidence rules. It contains 800 episodes, 120 byte-preserving interventions, and 1,155 blinded five-rater records, including a frozen extension with 114 supermajority pairs and 21 disagreement pairs. On the frozen sets of 114 preference pairs and 35 constraint interventions, the repeated absolute-score rubrics yield overlapping performance, with mean accuracies of 53.8-55.8% and three-call agreement of 29.8-32.5%, and their accuracy falls from 71.6-71.9% to 34.8-37.1% as the tie band widens. DirectPair-GLM reaches 85.1% preference accuracy, 89.5% constraint F1, and 81.9% Detect+Locate on the same items, and exact subpanel enumeration identifies four-of-five as the smallest stable human vote margin. Evaluation protocol, tie calibration, judge-call variation, and panel margin therefore affect performance as much as rubric design. We will release the specification packages, scripts, interventions, anonymized human votes and rationales, frozen judge runs, and analysis code.
evidence_items.title: DramaGrow: A Regime-Aware Benchmark for Auditing LLM Judges of Multi-Episode Drama

evidence_items.summary: Time Capsulo is a benchmark dataset for comparing the correctness and efficiency of AI-generated code with code written by humans before AI coding assistants. It contains 260 function-level tasks taken from 30 real open-source libraries whose releases date from 2018 to 2019. The tasks cover six languages: Python, Java, C++, JavaScript, Go and Rust. Each task is one real function, chosen by fixed rules. For every task the dataset provides a natural-language specification, the surrounding code context, a function stub, the original human-written function as the reference, the library version and commit, the covering tests, and seeded workloads (small, medium, large) with expected output digests. A model receives the prompt (specification, context and stub). Its answer is placed back into the original library, built in an era-appropriate Docker toolchain, and judged by the library's own tests and by an output-digest check. Only correct code is timed, so efficiency is never credited to wrong answers. The included harness measures runtime and peak memory. CPU energy can be measured on bare-metal Linux with RAPL support, following the procedure in the user guide (not automated in version 1.0). Library sources are not redistributed except for the function excerpts in the tasks: a setup script downloads each library at its pinned commit and verifies a content hash. The specifications were written with the help of a large language model and checked automatically for leakage and solvability. Licences: code is MIT; data and documentation are CC BY 4.0; third-party library excerpts keep their original licences (MIT, BSD-3-Clause, ISC, Apache-2.0), whose texts are included in the dataset.
evidence_items.title: Time Capsulo: A Sustainability Benchmark Dataset for Human and AI-Generated Code

evidence_items.summary: This dataset presents the first release of a living catalogue of publicly available data and information for further research on the 26 August 2026 Langtang Lirung disaster cascade. It brings together pre-event baselines, event observations and subsequent analyses to help researchers identify and access relevant material, assess its potential uses, and build on previous discovery work. The catalogue applies a scoping-review approach to identifying resources that can support future investigations of the event. The release contains 141 resource records and 5,883 associated asset records across eight thematic domains, following 74 documented searches through 24 September 2026 and source assessment completed on 28 September. The search and charting process is reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR. Records link sources and collections to their associated files, products, documents and services, preserving provenance, identifiers, geographic and temporal coverage, technical characteristics, access routes, reuse conditions and source limitations. The deposit includes the resource and asset inventory, search and assessment records, thematic and technical classifications, field documentation, and the data and scripts supporting catalogue analyses and figures. The online catalogue provides thematic discovery and access links, while the accompanying WebGIS enables geographic exploration where spatial information is available. Access to underlying third-party data and publications follows the provider links and conditions recorded in the catalogue. evidence_items.summary: Real-time embodied social interaction places two equally demanding requirements on an agent: continuously generating fluent multimodal interaction behavior, and proactively reasoning over accumulated dialogue and visual context to decide when to take initiative. These requirements must both be satisfied under a strict latency budget, making them difficult to meet simultaneously. We present ProAct , a dual-system framework that manages these time-critical requirements by integrating a low-latency Behavioral System for streaming multimodal interaction with a slower Cognitive System that performs long-horizon social reasoning and produces high-level proactive intentions. The Cognitive System incorporates an efficient memory mechanism and a user-motivation prediction module to reason over accumulated dialogue and visual context and determine when proactive intervention is appropriate. The Behavioral System further includes an intention-conditioned streaming flow-matching motion generator with a disentangled Control-Net branch, which translates deliberative intentions into continuous nonverbal behavior without disrupting interaction fluency. We deploy ProAct on a physical humanoid robot and validate the framework through comprehensive experiments, including real-world user studies, motion-generation benchmarks, and evaluation on ProActBench , a new, targeted benchmark for evaluating proactive trigger detection and restraint in embodied interaction. Code and ProActBench will be released at https://proactrobot.github.io/.
evidence_items.title: ProAct: Harnessing Streaming Motion Generation and Agentic Reasoning for Realtime Embodied Social Interaction

evidence_items.summary: Tuberculosis (TB) remains a major public-health challenge, particularly in settings where access to specialist radiological services and rapid diagnostic facilities is limited. Chest X-ray (CXR) imaging is widely used for pulmonary TB screening because it is comparatively accessible and can reveal radiographic abnormalities associated with the disease. However, many computer-aided detection systems primarily provide a classification score and offer limited information about the image regions influencing a prediction or the practical steps that should follow a screening result. This paper presents TB Care AI, an integrated artificial intelligence framework for explainable tuberculosis screening from chest X-ray images. The system combines an input-quality validation stage, a multi-task convolutional neural network (CNN), spatial segmentation, Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM), and a LLaMA 3 based conversational AI layer. The multi-task network performs diagnostic classification, pulmonary-zone or pathology prediction, and spatial segmenta-tion. A dual visual explanation mechanism combines segmenta-tion overlays and Grad-CAM attention maps. The conversational layer receives structured model outputs and transforms them into natural-language explanations and clinical decision-support information. The system also provides clinical report generation, temporary image handling, and healthcare-facility routing. On the reported evaluation benchmark, the framework achieved 98.40% accuracy, 97.60% precision, 98.80% sensitivity, 98.00% specificity, 98.20% F1-score, 98.56% F2-score, and a ROC-AUC of 0.992. The segmentation component achieved a Dice Similarity Coefficient of 91.40% and an Intersection over Union of 84.16%. The proposed platform is intended for screening and triage support and is not a substitute for formal clinical diagnosis or microbiological confirmation.
evidence_items.title: Explainable Tuberculosis Diagnosis from Chest X-rays Using Deep CNNs and LLaMA 3 Driven Conversational AI

evidence_items.summary: English abstract We develop a definition-driven, locally axiomatized framework for behavioral patterns for complete action processes and binary interaction. Shared foundations specify action agents, actions, evidence, content perspectives, partial identification, patterns, and conditional personality classification with distinct branch criteria. The complete-action branch organizes five functional blocks through 21 preference parameters, distinguishes a single action form from a conditionally stable pattern, and separates structural consistency from empirical frequency. Eight families contain 63 expanded configurations and 52 primary configurations. Family and configuration personality assignments require explicit structural and matching conditions; the catalogue is not a population taxonomy. Binary interaction constructs goal and evaluation patterns from distinct materials. Approach and avoidance each define 8 form and 9 impact-direction personality types, 34 entries across four catalogues; role evaluation yields 25 agent and 18 recipient types, 450 formal pairings, and 48 focused pairings. Traceable links preserve the distinction between wanted content, events that have occurred, and judgments. Complete actions enter these records through explicit action-event and action-goal links. Single joint records, sample identification within linked ranges, and joint personality descriptions occupy distinct levels without replacing one another's conditions. Under specified congruence axioms and non-degeneracy, a class-phase model has phase period five and requires at least five carrier classes. A shared application examines Big Five descriptions while retaining their measurement role. The framework supplies formal constructions and explicit undefined conditions; measurement validity, population distributions, longitudinal stability, and predictive gains require independent empirical tests.
evidence_items.title: Patterns of Behavior: Formal Structures of Complete Action Processes and Binary Interaction

evidence_items.summary: Scientific figures are the interface through which research claims are inspected and reused, but final published panels rarely expose the data or plotting code that produced them. Recovering this hidden provenance from pixels is therefore underdetermined. We introduce SciFigure2Code, an AI-reconstructed benchmark that evaluates presentation recovery: generating editable Python programs that preserve how a scientific panel is arranged and read. Role-specialized Codex agents generate, execute, visually refine, and audit silver-standard presentation programs that capture geometry, visual hierarchy, encodings, annotations, and typography. This reconstruction-and-audit protocol turns final published panels into auditable reference packages; the resulting resource contains 6,740 reviewed panels and SciFigureBench, a balanced 337-panel test set across 31 chart subtypes, five domains, and three complexity levels. Across 14 zero-shot models, execution and structural fidelity remain weak; a 328-panel full-figure study further exposes failures to locate and isolate requested panels. Claude Opus 4.7 leads image-only reconstruction, Claude Opus 4.6 leads caption-assisted reconstruction, and plan-then-code prompting improves all four tested models. SciFigure2Code provides an auditable testbed for constructing editable, visually faithful scientific figure presentations.
evidence_items.title: SciFigure2Code: An AI-Reconstructed Benchmark for Scientific Figure-to-Code

evidence_items.summary: This study examines whether large language models (LLMs) can perform audit work by comparing their performance with human learners, across model scale and under two enhancement techniques. Drawing on the audit-judgment distinction between declarative and procedural knowledge, the study evaluates seven publicly available LLMs on audit work in two forms of audit assessment. In the knowledge-based assessment, the LLMs answer four undergraduate auditing examinations previously sat by 352 accounting students, as a proxy of human learners. In the data-analytic case assessment, they plan and execute SQL-based substantive procedures to test the occurrence of revenue and the completeness of expenditures. On the knowledge-based assessment, LLMs outperform human learners where large LLMs typically fall between the 78th and 98th student percentiles, and large LLMs outperform small LLMs. On the data-analytic case assessment, no LLM scores above 50% of the rubric maximum, and large and small LLMs do not differ significantly. Meanwhile, two enhancement techniques: self-reflection and agentic workflow do not improve performance on the data-analytic case assessment. These results reveal a knowing–doing gap: LLMs display strong declarative audit knowledge but weak procedural capability, and self-correction without external feedback does not repair knowledge errors. This study discusses implications for audit practice, assessment design and standard setters.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Models In Auditing Assessments: Comparisons Between Human Learners, Model Scale, and Enhancement Techniques

evidence_items.summary: Legible robot motion should reveal the intended goal early while remaining collision-free and reasonably short. Under a small function-evaluation budget, however, continuous trajectory search leaves little room to discover intent-expressive motions through optimization alone. Standard population optimizers typically begin with random candidates, which provide numerical diversity but no scene-specific guidance for communicating intent. We evaluate a three-prior protected-greedy design under a shared low function-evaluation budget. We propose Protected-Prior Greedy Large-Language-Model-Seeded Grey Wolf Optimization (PPG-LLM-GWO). One structured large-language-model query returns confusion-aware, early-discrimination, and corridor-handling priors; after deterministic geometry repair, these trajectories occupy the three initial GWO leader roles, and 17 feasible-random trajectories complete the population. Subsequent sweeps protect the entering leaders, update only ordinary wolves, accept only feasibility-first improvements, and re-rank all survivors. We evaluate the method on a 24-map development bank at BFE∈{50,150}, using batch-aligned area under the best-so-far curve (AUC) after population initialization as the primary metric. Against original GWO, the development mean differences are +0.00222 [−0.00076, 0.00508] and +0.01040 [0.00543, 0.01616], respectively. The interval includes zero at BFE=50 but is above zero at BFE=150; PPG-LLM-GWO has the largest batch-aligned mean among the tested population optimizers at both settings. At BFE=50, the paired AUC differences versus PSO, DE, and GA are +0.02621, +0.01529, and +0.03349, respectively, with all three intervals above zero. At BFE=150, the differences are +0.01721, +0.02565, and +0.04954, respectively, and all four intervals, including the comparison with GWO, are above zero.
evidence_items.title: Protected-Prior Greedy Large-Language-Model-Seeded Grey Wolf Optimization for Low-Budget Legible Motion

evidence_items.summary: Streaming speech recognizers output a word only after the speaker has finished it, typically 90-400 ms later. For a voice agent every millisecond counts: the sooner the words are outputted, the sooner the agent can start a search or plan its reply. We present Earlybird, a 29M-parameter streaming recognizer (16.8 MB at 4 bits). Earlybird learns from audio cut off at random points, including partway through a word, and is asked to predict every word that is due by then in full, plus a guess of the next two words. Its raw token probabilities give a confidence for every word including the one still being spoken. On clean audiobook speech (LibriSpeech test-clean), the median word is predicted correctly 90 ms before the speaker finishes it, while released streaming models get it 90 to 400 ms after it ends. Earlybird is the earliest on all six test sets we time, covering audiobooks, TED talks, public speech, earnings calls, and synthetic speech. On the same audiobooks, 69% of words are predicted correctly before they end, against 3-25% for the other models. For words still being spoken, confidence is calibrated, with an expected calibration error (ECE) of 3.7 to 5.5. On the eight English Open ASR Leaderboard sets, it is more accurate than Moonshine Tiny on every set and roughly ties Whistle, a model of the same size.
evidence_items.title: Earlybird: Predictive Streaming Speech Recognition in 29M Parameters

evidence_items.summary: Typed-decision encoders answer a question about a text in one forward pass, but their behaviour outside English is rarely measured on a fixed yardstick. We release PolyRoute: 322 native-language support messages in 12 languages and 9 writing systems, 156 code-mixed or romanised messages (Hinglish, Spanglish, Arabizi), 967 optional native training rows, and a protocol for a three-way department-routing decision. Labels come from Qwen3.8-27B with a blind second pass (91% of candidates kept); an independent model, gemma4-31b, agrees on 97.2% of test items, and the largest character 5-gram similarity between any test text and any training text is 0.33. A leaderboard of 13 systems gives 61.2% for the English-root checkpoint, 77.3% for the shipped multilingual one and 96.6% for the best fine-tune; TF-IDF with logistic regression reaches 91.9%. On four withheld languages the three multilingual systems score 77%, 90% and 93%. On code-mixed text the English root (85%) is nominally ahead of the shipped multilingual checkpoint (79%; p=0.134). The split resolves differences only above about 4 points. All texts and labels are LLM-generated.

evidence_items.summary: Weight-space programming, introduced in recent MIT work by Takehi et al., enables a frontier LLM agent to read a network's weights and write a repair. Their GPT-6 Astra agent corrected the reasoning loops of Qwen3.5-0.8B without gradients, using 158 agent turns, 89.7 million tokens, and 50 forward-pass requests. Our method, Tree-Ising, casts this repair as a sparse discrete optimization problem over the model's own BF16 weights. Forward statistics define an objective that weakens a loop direction, strengthens a concluding direction, and preserves the layer's output on productive tokens. Within a state-tree representation, where lossless BF16 storage acts as a special case, the admissible edits are sign flips and exponent shifts that preserve all shared group exponents and mantissas. We decompose this objective exactly into independent QUBO (Ising) problems, one per output row, which we solve on a GPU using simulated annealing or quantum-inspired simulated bifurcation. On the agent's two layers, Tree-Ising achieves 54.6% on MATH-500, outperforming the agent's edit (51.7%) under the same evaluation protocol, while the base model scores 7.9% as reported. The simulated bifurcation solver yields a statistically indistinguishable repair at 55.1%. Both solvers outperform the agent edit across all five math benchmarks, with statistically significant improvements on MATH-500 and GSM8K after correcting for multiple comparisons. Our approach modifies 13% to 17% fewer weights and reduces BF16 bit flips by a factor of 2.2 to 2.3. It requires only four forward-pass requests and zero LLM tokens, with the annealing recipe costing about $0.90 in GPU time. On Qwen3.5-2B, with layers and dose selected using only the base model, the same recipe increases greedy GSM8K accuracy from 21.6% to 69.4%. As a proof of concept, we execute an eight-variable repair subproblem using QAOA on an IBM Heron processor.
evidence_items.title: Tree-Ising: Repairing Language Models with Bit-Level Ising Edits
