evidence_items.summary: Enterprise agents must determine whether ordinary requests are permitted by organizational records and policies while continuing legitimate work. We introduce DEPUTYBENCH, an executable benchmark with 79 base items, 375 instances, paired permission contexts, and graded evidence requirements. Across 12 models, revised audits give 88.0% pooled safety and 79.1% paired success. A controlled study of 28 derived tasks and six models tests authorization-fact flips, evidence masking, and irrelevant rewrites. Outcomes track backend permissions, yet restricted execution is more frequent with missing evidence than explicit non-permission: 10.3% versus 3.5% on 27 matched tasks, a 6.8-percentage-point difference (95% interval: 1.9-13.0; secondary analysis). A post-hoc analysis locates 61 of 100 masked-condition executions in four privacy tasks requiring complete cumulative counts or person-specific consent. The difference persists when the most error-prone model or the largest contributing task is excluded, but is much smaller outside those four tasks. Thus high safety with available evidence does not establish reliable stopping when permission cannot be verified. Mean paired success is equivalent within a prespecified five-point margin under irrelevant rewrites, while strong-model safety remains near ceiling. Scorer validation improves from 178 to 266 correctly scored cases out of 284 held-out counterexamples. Two security experts manually verified task ground truth over a two-week period; stage labels remain LLM-generated. The concentration analysis describes task structure and audited outcomes, not an identified internal mechanism.
evidence_items.title: DEPUTYBENCH: Evaluating Contextual Safety in Enterprise Agents

evidence_items.summary: The kinetic behaviour and environmental persistence of trinitrotoluene (TNT) under realistic marine conditions remain poorly understood. This study quantifies TNT dissolution, adsorption and transformation in controlled seawater systems representing shallow (≤200 m; photic) and deep (≥1000 m;aphotic) zones. Cylindrical TNT charges of mass range (1.17g –1.45 g) were immerged in 15 L of synthetic seawater (pH 8.1, salinity 35 ppt, 6–8 °C) with continuous flow and natural sediment for both photic and aphotic conditions respectively. TNT concentrations in water and sediment were monitored for 90days using HPLC and NMR analyses. Dissolution followed pseudo–first-order kinetics (r² ≥ 0.95), yielding solubility values 50.6–51.7 mg L⁻¹ and persistence times to 99.9% dissolution of 15.6 years (aphotic) and 26.5 years (photic). Aphotic systems exhibited dissolution limited behaviour with high mass recovery(95.9%). Illumination suppressed apparent dissolution and enhanced transformation and adsorption, lowering mass recovery to 75.3% and generating aminated and phenolic products e.g., amino-dinitrotoluene (ADNT), dinitrophenol (DNP), nitrotoluene (NT) via reduction, condensation and polymerisation inphotic conditions. The integrated kinetic and mass balance framework provides quantitative parameters and mechanistic insight necessary for fate modelling, environmental risk assessment and management of legacy underwater munitions in marine environments.
evidence_items.title: Dataset supporting Quantitative evaluation of the fate of TNT in controlled photic and aphotic zones: Implications for environmental risk assessment of underwater munitions

evidence_items.summary: Selecting vision-language models to annotate specialized-domain images requires evidence that general-purpose benchmarks may not provide: current domain knowledge, correct domain con-cepts, and restraint where the image is inconclusive. We present a profile-first protocol for pre-deployment evaluation and instantiate it as the Handball Knowledge Benchmark (HKB). HKB separately evaluates productive terminology, rules and tactics, and both general and hand-ball-specific interpretation of images. Diagnostics cover rule currency, answer-order robustness, fabrication and warranted abstention. A provider-diverse judge panel with provider-aware recusal scores open-ended responses. Among the 19 ranked multimodal candidates, GPT-5.6 Sol led all four dimensions (G1 0.97, G2 98.8%, G3 8.22/7.98), but below it ranks order depended on dimension weighting. Diagnostics exposed mismatches hidden by aggregate scores: high rules accuracy coex-isted with superseded rule knowledge, reliable sport recognition with scarce warranted abstention under ambiguity, and near-identical general visual scores with a 1.6-point gap in handball-specific interpretation. Results were stable across judges and aggregation rules. Under an illustrative deci-sion rule, six admissible candidates differed about threefold in inference cost. Therefore, we suggest displaying domain competencies as a profile and not as a rank, while the protocol can be transferred to other domains by replacing the handball content.
evidence_items.title: Profile-First Model Selection for Specialized Image Annotation: A Handball Knowledge Benchmark for Vision-Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Binaural audio is a practical spatial audio format for headphone playback and is widely used in immersive media such as games, VR/AR, and interactive multimedia. Currently, binaural audio is still largely obtained either by specialized recordings or by spatializing pre-recorded monaural signals, which limits flexibility for controllable content creation. While recent text-to-audio models can generate the required audio, most of them target monaural output or unconstrained stereo. They provide limited control over spatial attributes such as direction and motion. To address these challenges, we propose BinauralLM, a spatial prompted text-to-binaural audio generation framework with large language model (LLM). BinauralLM adopts a two-stage pipeline. First, we use a Qwen2.5 LLM to autoregressively generate coarse binaural token sequences conditioned on text and spatial prompts. To effectively couple semantic content with spatial cues, we introduce a spatial prompt encoder and an attention fusion module to produce a unified conditioning representation for binaural token generation. Second, we employ a flow matching model that takes the coarse binaural tokens as conditions and reconstructs high-quality binaural waveforms in the continuous domain. Experimental results on the BEWO-1M dataset demonstrate that BinauralLM achieves superior performance on standard text-to-audio metrics and binaural spatial metrics, and achieves higher MOS scores in perceptual evaluation, especially on spatialization quality. These results indicate that our proposed method offers an effective route to controllable and high-quality text-to-binaural audio generation.
evidence_items.title: BinauralLM: spatial prompted text-to-binaural audio generation with large language model

evidence_items.summary: Large language models can combine inference steps governed by different logical semantics, so locally valid steps may still form an invalid reasoning chain. MetaPCR-LLM represents such chains as typed, labeled proof graphs and checks transfers between native validators. Across four constructed or transformed hallucination datasets, it improves pooled hallucination F1 from 0.77 to 0.83 relative to ValidLLP-style validation, while also improving step-validity and chain-certification decisions. On independently annotated ProcessBench, RAGTruth, and ProofWriter samples, it improves error detection, contextual hallucination detection, and query accuracy, respectively, over the matched ValidLLP-style comparator. In mixed-logic cases, disabling bridge checks reduces performance, indicating that locally accepted steps require explicit composition checks. Error analysis identifies decomposition, routing, and formalization as continuing sources of failure; specialist methods also retain advantages on some tasks. Validation incurs a modest latency increase. These findings support cross-logic composition checks in the evaluated settings, while formal guarantees remain conditional on encoded premises, supported fragments, and trusted checking procedures.
evidence_items.title: MetaPCR-LLM: Universal Proof-Carrying Reasoning Across Heterogeneous Logics for Large Language Model Validation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) have significantly advanced various domains such as healthcare, cybersecurity, and natural language processing. However, their practical deployment is often hindered by hallucinations-instances where the models produce inaccurate or misleading outputs. This study presents a robust CNN-based multimodal framework that integrates Red Teaming for adversarial testing, Prompt Engineering for refined input guidance, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) to enhance factual accuracy through real-time information retrieval. The framework processes diverse data modalities including text, audio, and images, leveraging convolutional neural networks for effective feature extraction and alignment. Experimental validation on a synthesized multimodal dataset demonstrates a test accuracy of 75% after 50 training epochs, with notable performance metrics such as a ROC-AUC of 0.93 on neuroimaging data, an F1-score of 0.85 for mobile sensing, and a BLEU score of 0.94 for multilingual translation tasks. These results affirm the framework’s capability in reducing hallucinations across varied modalities and noisy, imbalanced datasets. The proposed approach paves the way for more dependable LLM applications in real-world settings, though future work will focus on integrating transformer architectures and expanding domain-specific datasets to further enhance scalability and precision.
evidence_items.title: A Multimodal Framework Using Red Teaming Prompt Engineering and Retrieval Augmented Generation to Mitigate Large Language Model Hallucinations

evidence_items.summary: Background/Objectives: Children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) commonly experience feeding- and nutrition-related problems, while families increasingly encounter large language model (LLM)-based tools as sources of health information. Evidence on the reliability of these tools for ASD-specific medical nutrition therapy (MNT) remains limited. The aim of this study is to compare the responses of four publicly available LLM-based platform configurations to nutrition questions related to ASD in terms of quality, guideline compliance, readability, and hallucination. Methods: In this cross-sectional comparative benchmark study, 60 standardized, unbiased informational questions across five MNT domains (12 per domain) were each submitted once in separate sessions to four LLM-based platform configurations: ChatGPT, ChatGPT Plus, Microsoft Copilot, and Google Gemini, yielding 240 responses. Only one response was evaluated for each question-platform combination, and variability between repeated productions was not measured. Four nutrition and dietetics experts, blinded to platform identity, assessed response quality using Medical Artificial Intelligence Quality Analysis (QAMAI) and Global Quality Score (GQS), and reviewed compliance with NICE guidelines and the American Academy of Pediatrics clinical report, and evaluated readability and binary hallucination classifications. QAMAI, GQS, and guideline-concordance scores were compared using generalized estimating equations with a Gamma distribution and a log link. Results: Platform, domain (D), and platform × domain effects were significant for QAMAI, GQS, and guideline concordance (all omnibus p < 0.05). ChatGPT Plus had the highest overall mean QAMAI, GQS, and guideline-concordance scores. Gemini showed relatively high quality ratings but the lowest overall concordance with guidelines. In the analyzed response set, no hallucinations were detected in either the ChatGPT or ChatGPT Plus configurations (0/60 each; 0%).
evidence_items.title: Evaluating Large Language Model Platforms for Medical Nutrition Therapy in Autism Spectrum Disorder: Quality, Guideline Concordance, Readability, and Hallucinations

evidence_items.summary: Objective: Artificial intelligence (AI) represents a potentially transformative tool in assisted reproductive technology (ART), particularly in vitro fertilization (IVF), for gamete assessment, embryo selection, non-invasive genetic testing, and laboratory automation. This scoping review synthesized recent evidence on AI applications in IVF laboratories and evaluated their translational maturity using an evidence maturity framework and a strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats (SWOT) analysis.Methods: This scoping review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) Extension for Scoping Reviews guidelines. PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were searched for peer-reviewed studies published from January 2020 to February 2025. Eligible studies evaluated AI, machine learning, or deep learning in laboratory components of ART. Data were charted on AI methods, dataset characteristics, validation strategies, clinical endpoints, and performance metrics.Results: Ninety-four studies were included. Most applications addressed embryo grading and implantation prediction using convolutional neural networks and were evaluated through internal cross-validation. Reported areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve ranged from 0.75 to 0.92, depending on the endpoint and dataset size. AI applications in sperm analysis and oocyte assessment showed greater reproducibility than manual evaluation. Non-invasive genetic prediction models displayed promising but heterogeneous sensitivity and remained predominantly limited to internal validation. Few studies reported prospective evaluation or external validation using multicenter datasets.Conclusion: AI applications in IVF are expanding, but most remain at early stages of clinical translation. Standardized datasets, external validation, interpretable algorithms, and regulatory oversight remain necessary for safe, equitable clinical integration.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence in the in vitro fertilization laboratory: A scoping review and SWOT-based evaluation of emerging applications

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Meeting Paris-aligned trajectories in the Global South requires rapid, data-intensive coordination of where and how low-carbon energy infrastructure is built, yet the underlying data are fragmented across sovereign jurisdictions reluctant to pool sensitive energy, land and infrastructure information. Wealthy blocs are answering their own version of this problem with shared or sovereign compute at extraordinary cost — a €10-billion European network of publicly funded ‘AI Factories’ and a US$500-billion private buildout in the United States — scales no developing country can replicate alone. Federated learning (FL), in which institutions jointly train a shared model by exchanging model parameters rather than raw data, offers an alternative technical foundation, but its value for cross-country energy modelling in developing regions has not been quantified. Treating 44 Global South countries (16,404 operating facilities) in the Global Energy Monitor Global Integrated Power Tracker as sovereign data silos, we benchmarked four training regimes on a geospatial renewable-versus-fossil classification task. Federated averaging matched centralized pooling of all raw data to three decimal places (AUC 0.895 versus 0.895) while no record left its country of origin, and personalized FL exceeded isolated national training (0.910 versus 0.905; two-sided Wilcoxon p = 0.048), with the advantage larger on average among data-poor silos and widening as training data were artificially restricted. Independent replication on the 2021 WRI Global Power Plant Database (31 silos, 6,545 plants) reproduces the sovereignty result, though there the personalization advantage is statistically indistinguishable from zero.
evidence_items.title: Federated learning reconciles data sovereignty with collaborative energy-transition modelling across the Global South: a public-data benchmark anchored in Indonesia

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Phenomic prediction (PP) is a genetic value prediction method inspired by genomic prediction (GP). One key feature of PP compared to GP is its potential ability to predict interactions between genotypes and environments (GxE). Using kernel-based models, many relationship matrix calculation methods for the G and GxE terms have been proposed but never fairly compared. In this study, we exhaustively tested different combinations of published methods to compute these matrices, and implemented a new method supposed to better split the genetic (G) and GxE information in their respective matrices. Using three datasets on maize, rice, and triticale, results show that the G effect matrix is the main driver of predictive abilities (PA). Computing the G effect matrix using BLUPs of wavelengths across environments was better when predicting new genotypes in known environments. To predict known genotypes in new environments or in a sparse testing scenario, it was better to compute one relationship matrix per environment and average them into a single G effect matrix. We found little differences between models including a GxE term and models without it. Nevertheless, dense GxE matrices including relationships within and across environments were generally the best choice. Finally, combining genomic information for the G effect, and phenomic information for the GxE effect gave the best results. Clear guidance of the best ways to take advantage of phenomic prediction to predict GxE will likely require a simulation approach to better control the GxE information in datasets.
evidence_items.title: Predicting GxE through phenomic prediction: A benchmark study across three species

evidence_items.summary: Abstract We present MultiLoKo, a new benchmark for evaluating multilinguality in LLMs covering 31 languages. MultiLoKo consists of three partitions: a main partition with 500 questions per language, separately sourced to be locally relevant to the specific language, and two translated partitions, containing human-authored translations from 30 non-English languages to English and vice versa. For comparison, we also release corresponding machine-authored translations. The data is equally distributed over two splits: a dev split and a blind, out-of-distribution test split. MultiLoKo can be used to study a variety of questions regarding the multilinguality of LLMs as well as meta-questions about multilingual benchmark creation. We compute MultiLoKo scores for 11 base and chat models marketed to be multilingual and study their average performance, their performance parity across languages, how much their ability to answer questions depends on the question language, and which languages are most difficult. We find that none of the models we evaluated perform well on MultiLoKo, as indicated by low average scores as well as large differences between the best and worst scoring languages. Furthermore, we find a substantial effect of the question language, indicating suboptimal knowledge transfer between languages. Lastly, we find that using local vs. English-translated data can result in differences of more than 20 points for the best performing models, drastically changing the estimated difficulty of some languages. For using machines instead of human translations, we find a weaker effect on ordering of language difficulty, a larger difference in model rankings, and a substantial drop in estimated performance for all models.
evidence_items.title: MultiLoKo: A Multilingual Local Knowledge Benchmark for LLMs Spanning 31 Languages

evidence_items.summary: Classifiers of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) from resting state functional MRI rarely generalize across sites, and many reported accuracies are inflated by data leakage.We show that an agentic artificial intelligence framework, ASD Neuro Agentic (ANA), whose language model agents propose features from the literature and researcher input while fixed tools perform every calculation, can search auditably for site independent classifiers while controlling the leakage. In 1,028 participants from 17 ABIDE I centers, ANA tested 71 pipelines and selected a ComBat harmonized ensemble of tangent space connectivity models from six parcellations and 98 public connectivity derivatives. In leave one center out testing, the ensemble reached an area under the curve of 0.814 (95% CI, 0.773 to 0.841), outperforming ASD DiagNet and ASD SAENet. Predictive connectivity was mainly reduced in ASD. Agentic AI offers a systematic and efficient approach to exploring, evaluating, and identifying pipelines as model selection grows complex.
evidence_items.title: ASD Neuro Agentic (ANA): An Agentic Framework for Feature Discovery and Cross Site Generalization in Autism fMRI Classification

evidence_items.summary: Maps of political regimes usually sort countries into democracies and autocracies. I classify the constitutional form of all 197 states (the 193 UN members, the Holy See, Palestine, Taiwan and Kosovo) on eight features: the kind of head of state, how that office is filled, the executive type (including the premier-presidential and president-parliamentary subtypes of semi-presidentialism), whether head of state and head of government are one office, the territorial structure, the number of chambers, the electoral system of the lower or only chamber and any power sharing fixed by community. Each field is derived by stated rules from two independent sources, V-Dem v16 (latest year 2025) and the CIA World Factbook (2026 and 2024 editions), compared cell by cell, with 83 documented and cited hand decisions. The countries fall into 12 families and 112 exact systems, of which 80 belong to a single country; those 80 countries hold 42% of the world's population. The largest shared system, unitary parliamentary republics with one chamber elected by list proportional representation, has 14 members. Presidential republics (52) and parliamentary republics (45) are the largest families and each holds over a quarter of humanity; 25 federations hold 41%. Set against V-Dem's Regimes of the World, 71% of countries electing their lower house by proportional representation are democracies against 43% of majoritarian ones, 78% of premier-presidential against 11% of president-parliamentary systems, and ceremonial monarchies have the highest mean Liberal Democracy Index of any family (0.64). These patterns are descriptive. The classification, sources and decisions are released as open data. Interactive version: https://maps.tristanhotham.com/government-types/ . Data and code: https://github.com/Tristan-Hotham/government-types . Blog post: https://blog.tristanhotham.com/2026/10/31/government-types/. Data: V-Dem Country-Year Dataset v16 (Coppedge et al.
evidence_items.title: How the World Is Governed: A Feature-by-Feature Classification of 197 Systems of Government, Cross-Checked against V-Dem and the CIA World Factbook

evidence_items.summary: ExpertCrowd-SWE (EC-SWE) is a benchmark of 100 expert-authored, multi-file software engineering tasks for evaluating autonomous coding agents in large, unfamiliar codebases. Each task is a change request written by a practising engineer against a pinned commit of a real repository, paired with a sealed reference solution and a task-specific grader whose weighted, mostly executable criteria award partial credit; must-pass blockers and pass/fail gates encode what a maintainer would refuse to merge. The tasks span 87 open-source projects and 11 languages. The median ticket is 148 words, while the median reference solution changes 471 lines. Every task image is calibrated before release so that the reference solution scores 1.0 and both the untouched repository and an inert change score 0; nearly half of the tasks also ship alternative, lazy and adversarial control patches that the grader must classify correctly. The final 100 tasks were selected for difficulty against current frontier models. We evaluate seven frontier models, five runs each (3,495 scored runs), in a single platform harness that gives each model its provider-native tool interface. Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3%) and GPT-6 Astra (63.7%) lead without a statistically significant gap, followed by Claude Fable 5.1 (46.5%), Gemini 3.8 Flash (40.0%), and a statistically indistinguishable group of Qwen 3.8 Max, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Grok 4.6 (32-34%). No task is fully solved by every model, and on 80 tasks no model earns full credit on all five runs. Scores span 35 points. Depending on the model, agents take a median of 33 to 166 steps per run, with little relation to score. We release 24 tasks with their environments, graders and results, and hold out 76 to limit contamination.
evidence_items.title: ExpertCrowd-SWE: Measuring Frontier Coding Agents on Expert-Authored Engineering Tasks in Unfamiliar Codebases

evidence_items.summary: Despite rapid advances in large language models (LLMs), their deployment in the sports and health domain remains high-risk due to the absence of domain-specific evaluation benchmarks. Existing general-purpose benchmarks (e.g., MMLU and HELM) primarily assess broad knowledge and reasoning capabilities, but fail to capture critical domain requirements such as exercise safety, physiological appropriateness, personalization, and actionable coaching quality. This gap is particularly concerning in fitness and health applications, where incorrect or unsafe recommendations can lead to physical harm. To address this limitation, we introduce MoveBench, the first comprehensive benchmarking framework specifically designed for evaluating LLMs in sports and health coaching. The proposed benchmark integrates heterogeneous task formats, including multiple-choice questions (MCQs) and open-ended question answering (OpenQA), grounded in real-world user scenarios and paired with structured rubrics emphasizing safety compliance, scientific validity, and training logic. Through large-scale evaluation of 15 diverse LLMs on 809 questions with 5,012 rubric-level criteria, our results reveal substantial performance variability, particularly in safety awareness, structured program design, and personalization capability, highlighting a critical gap between knowing and doing. Our work establishes a foundational evaluation standard for sports and health LLM applications and provides a reproducible framework for advancing safe, reliable, and context-aware AI-driven coaching systems. Open resources are available at https://github.com/SatoSakula/MoveBench.
evidence_items.title: MoveBench: A Rubric-Based Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models in Sports and Health Coaching

evidence_items.summary: Recovering high-quality images from degraded underwater observations is crucial for underwater exploration. Polarization observations show promise as an effective source of complementary physical cues for recovering target radiance under clear-water conditions. However, existing methods have yet to jointly model raw intensity information and polarization cues to enable image restoration driven by an understanding of mixed underwater degradations. To overcome these limitations, we propose DORIS, a unified multimodal language-driven framework that jointly uses polarization and RGB information to generate textual descriptions of degradation types and severity levels through structured semantic instructions and enhances joint restoration representations under the guidance of degradation-aware semantic features to improve restoration robustness under mixed degradations. We further construct a new benchmark named MixPolar, which contains underwater images exhibiting real degradations and the corresponding annotations. It supports systematic evaluation of degradation perception, image restoration, and downstream task performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method effectively integrates polarization and RGB information, achieving competitive performance in degradation perception and image restoration.
evidence_items.title: DORIS: Polarization Aware Multimodal Degradation Perception for Underwater Image Restoration

evidence_items.summary: Modern agentic workflows decompose user requests into sequences of tool calls with correctly resolved parameters, the results of which are processed through reasoning traces in the language model's context window. The prevailing route to improving such reasoning is test-time scaling, which trains models to search over long chains of thought; but the resulting capability is entangled in model weights, cannot be checked step by step, and is costly at inference. We present Forethought, a neurosymbolic reasoning system built from a library of symbolic and neural primitives composed through a typed domain-specific language. The results are reasoning programs: concrete representations of the model's work, in which every step carries an output contract that is checked at design time and enforced at execution time. Symbolic steps hold by construction, while learned steps are contract-checked and empirically validated, giving an explicit boundary between what is guaranteed and what is measured. Instantiated as a tool-calling execution kernel and evaluated on four standard tool-calling benchmark suites, Forethought improves end-to-end accuracy by a median of 32% relative to prompting the same base model directly, and reaches the highest aggregate accuracy among the evaluated configurations, though only by a margin within single-run noise over a frontier model. Systems pairing small open models with Forethought's fixed small-model layer match that frontier model, and a pipeline with a non-reasoning responder outperforms its reasoning sibling while requiring only a single fine-tuning stage. Removing the contract-and-control layer erases most of these gains, showing that checked structure, not decomposition alone, drives the improvement. Our results show the potential of rich symbolic orchestrators for building language-model agents that are more accurate, reliable, and auditable.
evidence_items.title: Forethought: Verifiable Reasoning from Neurosymbolic Primitive Programming

evidence_items.summary: Text-to-image (T2I) generation models have achieved remarkable progress in producing visually realistic images from natural language prompts. Yet it remains unclear whether their success reflects genuine causal understanding or sophisticated pattern matching over visual-textual correlations. Inspired by Russell's inductivist turkey, we introduce Counterfactual-World (CF-World), a counterfactual benchmark designed to investigate whether text-to-image models can generate images under rules that systematically contradict real-world priors. CF-World organizes each scenario into three progressive levels: factual generation under ordinary world knowledge, explicit counterfactual generation with direct visual instructions, and implicit counterfactual generation requiring causal deduction from altered rules. We evaluate open-source and closed-source text-to-image models using CF-Eval, a scoring pipeline based on vision-language models. We report the scores at each prompt level as the primary results and use Prior Resistance Rate (PRR) and Reasoning Retention Rate (RRR) as auxiliary descriptive indicators. All evaluated models score lower on counterfactual prompts than on factual prompts. Diagnostic experiments reveal difficulties in following altered rules and recombining rarely co-occurring visual attributes. The gains from rephrasing object and attribute names are consistent with a role for learned visual priors in counterfactual generation. Our benchmark and evaluation code are publicly available at https://jylei16.github.io/CF-World.github.io/.
evidence_items.title: Are Text-to-Image Models Inductivist Turkeys? A Counterfactual Benchmark for Causal Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Commonsense knowledge is widely used to support multimodal reasoning and generation, yet existing resources are predominantly text-only and lack grounding in visual context. This limitation often leads to the retrieval of semantically related but visually misaligned knowledge, and can degrade downstream performance. We introduce MMCOMET, a large-scale multimodal commonsense knowledge graph that integrates physical, social, and eventive knowledge with visual grounding. MMCOMET extends ATOMIC2020 by associating each commonsense triple with representative images through a hybrid alignment pipeline, resulting in over 900K multimodal tuples spanning 19 relation types. We further establish a unified evaluation framework across diverse vision-language tasks, including visual commonsense reasoning, visual question answering, visual storytelling, image editing, and image captioning. Our analysis shows that multimodal grounding provides more contextually aligned and reliable knowledge compared to both text-only knowledge graphs and LLM-based knowledge generation, particularly in reasoning-intensive scenarios. At the same time, we observe that the effectiveness of external knowledge is task-dependent, and naive knowledge integration can introduce noise in perception-dominated settings. To mitigate this, we propose an adaptive knowledge router that dynamically selects optimal paths or bypass knowledge in harmful settings. MMCOMET provides a scalable multimodal commonsense resource and a benchmark for studying the role of grounded knowledge in multimodal systems.
evidence_items.title: MMCOMET: A Large-Scale Multimodal Commonsense Knowledge Graph for Visual Reasoning

evidence_items.summary: Large language models have transformed code generation, enabling unprecedented automation in software development. As mobile ecosystems evolve, HarmonyOS has emerged as a critical platform requiring robust development tools. Software development for the HarmonyOS ecosystem relies heavily on ArkTS, a statically typed extension of TypeScript. Despite its growing importance, the ecosystem lacks robust tools for automated code repair, primarily due to the absence of a high-quality benchmark for evaluation. To address this gap, we present ArkEval, a unified framework for ArkTS automated repair workflow evaluation and benchmark construction. It provides the first comprehensive benchmark specifically designed for ArkTS automated program repair. We constructed this benchmark by mining issues from a large-scale official Huawei repository containing over 400 independent ArkTS applications. Through a rigorous multi-stage filtering process, we curated 502 reproducible issues. To ensure testability, we employed a novel LLM-based test generation and voting mechanism involving Claude and other models. Furthermore, we standardized problem statements to facilitate fair evaluation. Finally, we evaluated four state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs) on our benchmark using a retrieval-augmented repair workflow. Our results highlight the current capabilities and limitations of LLMs in repairing ArkTS code, paving the way for future research in this low-resource language domain.
evidence_items.title: ArkEval: Benchmarking and Evaluating Automated CodeRepair for ArkTS

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) achieve strong performance in long-horizon agentic tasks through multi-step interaction and reasoning at test time. However, repeatedly invoking these models incurs substantial inference cost over an episode. Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces this cost, but using a fixed low precision throughout an episode can sharply lower task success. We observe that interaction steps differ sharply in their sensitivity to quantization: given the same context, decoding a step at low precision turns a success into a failure at only about 1% of the steps, which we call critical steps. Based on this observation, we propose Dynamic Mixed-Precision Routing (DMR), a framework that adaptively selects between high-precision and low-precision versions of the same LLM at each decision step. Leveraging an entire-space factorization to jointly predict a step's divergence and its effect on the outcome, DMR learns to recognize these critical steps by training only a lightweight router on the model's hidden state. By reusing a shared high-precision KV cache and the hidden states, DMR avoids redundant context prefill and a separate text encoder, enabling precision switching with less than 1 ms of overhead per step and adding less than 0.11% to step latency for routing. This mixed-precision design also enables nested quantization, reducing the memory footprint by 39% on average compared with FP16. Across three long-horizon agentic benchmarks with nested quantization, DMR achieves an average 2.44x decode speedup over FP16 at comparable task success rates, without fine-tuning the underlying model. On ALFWorld with GPTQ, DMR achieves a 1.71x decode speedup with 86.9% success, compared with 87.2% for FP16.
evidence_items.title: Dynamic Mixed-Precision Routing for Efficient Multi-step LLM Interaction

evidence_items.summary: Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP) is a key procedure in the diagnosis and treatment of biliary and pancreatic diseases. Artificial intelligence has been pointed as one solution to automatize diagnosis. However, public ERCP datasets are scarce, which limits the use of such approach. Therefore, this study aims to help fill this gap by providing a large and curated dataset. The collection is composed of 19.018 raw images and 19.317 processed from 1.602 patients. 5.519 images are labeled, which provides a ready to use dataset. All images were manually inspected and annotated by two gastroenterologist with more than 5 years of experience and reviewed by another gastroenterologist with more than 20 years of experience, all with more than 400 ERCP procedures annually. The utility and validity of the dataset is proven by a classification experiment. This collection aims to provide or contribute for a benchmark in automatic ERCP analysis and diagnosis of biliary and pancreatic diseases.
evidence_items.title: Curated endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography images dataset

evidence_items.summary: One of the largest drivers of social inequality is unequal access to personal tutoring, with wealthier individuals able to afford it, while the majority cannot. Affordable, effective AI tutors offer a scalable solution. We focus on adaptive learning, predicting whether a student will answer a question correctly, a key component of any effective tutoring system. Yet many platforms struggle to achieve high prediction accuracy, especially in data-sparse settings. To address this, we release the largest open dataset of professionally marked formal mathematics exam responses to date. We introduce a probabilistic modelling framework rooted in Item Response Theory (IRT) that achieves over 80 percent accuracy, setting a new benchmark for mathematics prediction accuracy of formal exam papers. Extending this, our collaborative filtering models incorporate topic-level skill profiles, but reveal a surprising and educationally significant finding, a single latent ability parameter alone is needed to achieve the maximum predictive accuracy. Our main contribution though is deriving and implementing a novel discrete variational inference framework, achieving our highest prediction accuracy in low-data settings and outperforming all classical IRT and matrix factorisation baselines.
evidence_items.title: Accurate Predictions in Education with Discrete Variational Inference

evidence_items.summary: R analysis code and summary result tables for the paper “Metabolic gene-expression scores add no prognostic information on late recurrence of ER-positive breast cancer: a multicohort, multi-omic study”. The study tests whether gene-expression scores of four metabolic programs (glycolysis, fatty acid oxidation, oxidative phosphorylation and the lysosome), 159 metabolic pathways and 2319 metabolic genes in the primary tumour carry information on distant recurrence after 5 years in ER-positive/HER2-negative breast cancer (METABRIC, with external MetaGxBreast cohorts and GSE17705). It also examines what the scores measure (variance decomposition, split-half reliability, matched metabolite levels, copy number) and compares them with random gene sets of the same size. Contents: analysis and figure scripts (folder scripts/), summary result tables needed to run the figure and table scripts (folder 04 tables/), gene-set definitions (gene symbols only) and the cohort and covariate tables derived from the open clinical data. The README describes the data sources, the order in which to run the scripts, and which script produces each figure and table. METABRIC gene expression data are under controlled access (European Genome-phenome Archive) and are not included. Changes in this version: the figure and table numbering follows the published paper; Figure 1 and Figure 5 labels updated; new script for Supplementary Fig. S16; the random-gene-set benchmark script no longer writes the size-matched Hallmark comparison or the former four-panel figure (the Hallmark subsets are still drawn, so that the random-number sequence and all reported values are unchanged); Supplementary Table S4 updated. The changed scripts were run again from this repository and reproduced the published output tables. Licence: MIT.

evidence_items.summary: Domain-specific languages (DSLs) are widely used in enterprise software, giving a compact interface to complex tasks, from data access to infrastructure automation. Platforms increasingly extend them to agents, where a developer declares the topics, permitted actions, and guardrails of an agent rather than writing general-purpose code. Large language models (LLMs) write general-purpose code well, but that ability has been measured almost entirely on languages abundant in public pretraining data, and enterprise DSLs are neither abundant nor public. We introduce AgentScript-Eval, an execution-graded benchmark of 100 real tasks for AgentScript, the declarative DSL that Salesforce uses in Agentforce to build conversational agents. Tasks span authoring an agent from a specification, debugging a broken definition, and optimizing a working one. Evaluating five models zero-shot, we find that the regime is hard: the best model reaches only 25.0% pass@3, and every model scores 0% on authoring from scratch. We further find that model scale and price are weak predictors of success -- a 31B open-weight model attains the highest compilation rate of any model tested (48.0%) and matches the strongest frontier model on partial-credit accuracy at the lowest token cost. Adding an agentic compile-and-edit loop is the single largest lever, roughly doubling partial-credit accuracy. Beyond that gain, the wording of domain guidance matters more than its packaging. The same skill pack scores 28% as plain documentation but only 14% as a live plugin. Rewriting one skill inside that plugin then raises it to 37%, our best result, with catalog and tooling untouched. Larger models did not reliably outperform smaller ones; what mattered was the harness surrounding the model and the guidance supplied to it.
evidence_items.title: AgentScript-Eval: Benchmarking LLMs and Agents for Code Generation in an Enterprise DSL

evidence_items.summary: RESEARCH COLLECTION / FLAGSHIPS 51–60 OF 90 Botanical Skin Science & Nano-Quantum Research Validation at the Limit STARLI Herbal Skincare | F51–F60 / 90 | Author 33 | Research Design Working Edition v1.2 This ten-volume prospective, nonclinical research-design collection examines herbal cellular stress, nanocarrier immune interactions, circadian repair, multiomics ageing markers and skin-state digital twins, then connects quantum-assisted compound screening with microrobotic monitoring, regenerative-biomaterial qualification, cumulative exposure safety and integrated evidence platforms. Each flagship poses a different falsifiable scientific contract rather than a claim of demonstrated cosmetic or clinical efficacy. Two five-theme units contain ten English 777-page editions: 300 conditional formula plates, 820 chapter openings, 4,100 separately paginated study designs, 2,000 Research Gates and 330 Phoenix Answer Embryos. The v1.2 second-pass Gate revision is editorial research design; structural counts and textual uniqueness do not demonstrate experimental validity. Research Unit I · F51–F55 F51 HERBAL BIOACTIVES AND SKIN CELLULAR STRESS RESPONSES AT THE LIMIT — Tests paired heat-shock and viable-cell responses through orthogonal LC-MS and ELISA, including pigment-matched vehicle blanks. Botanical fluorescence may mimic lower stress, so assay interference and sample identity must be excluded. Irreversible heat injury or loss of viable-cell identity stops acceptance. F52 NANODELIVERY SYSTEMS AND THE CUTANEOUS IMMUNE INTERFACE AT THE LIMIT — Relates cytokine response to verified internalized carrier mass in blinded, endotoxin-negative and equal-dose free-active comparisons. Free active or endotoxin may explain immune activation without a carrier-specific effect. Unexcluded immune activation and unresolved nanocarrier mass balance prevent release.
evidence_items.title: RESEARCH COLLECTION / FLAGSHIPS 51–60 OF 90 Botanical Skin Science & Nano-Quantum Research Validation at the Limit STARLI Herbal Skincare  |  F51–F60 / 90  |  Author 33  |  Research Design Working Edition v1.2 This ten-volume prospective, nonclinical research-design collection examines herbal cellular stress, nanocarrier immune interactions, circadian repair, multiomics ageing markers and skin-state digital twins, then connects quantum-assisted compound screening with microrobotic monitoring, regenerative-biomaterial qualification, cumulative exposure safety and integrated evidence platforms. Each flagship poses a different falsifiable scientific contract rather than a claim of demonstrated cosmetic or clinical efficacy. Two five-theme units contain ten English 777-page editions: 300 conditional formula plates, 820 chapter openings, 4,100 separately paginated study designs, 2,000 Research Gates and 330 Phoenix Answer Embryos. The v1.2 second-pass Gate revision is editorial research design; structural counts and textual uniqueness do not demonstrate experimental validity. Research Unit I · F51–F55 F51  HERBAL BIOACTIVES AND SKIN CELLULAR STRESS RESPONSES AT THE LIMIT — Tests paired heat-shock and viable-cell responses through orthogonal LC-MS and ELISA, including pigment-matched vehicle blanks. Botanical fluorescence may mimic lower stress, so assay interference and sample identity must be excluded. Irreversible heat injury or loss of viable-cell identity stops acceptance. F52  NANODELIVERY SYSTEMS AND THE CUTANEOUS IMMUNE INTERFACE AT THE LIMIT — Relates cytokine response to verified internalized carrier mass in blinded, endotoxin-negative and equal-dose free-active comparisons. Free active or endotoxin may explain immune activation without a carrier-specific effect. Unexcluded immune activation and unresolved nanocarrier mass balance prevent release. F53  SKIN REPAIR SIGNALING AND CIRCADIAN BIOLOGY AT THE LIMIT — Tests phase-stratified repair proxies by randomizing masked sampling times within identical cell batches. Culture age and collection order may masquerade as circadian biology; clock-matched controls are required. Missing time-matched references or severe stress responses terminate the proposed comparison. F54  SKIN AGING BIOMARKERS AND MULTIOMICS ANALYSIS AT THE LIMIT — Challenges out-of-batch biomarker probability calibration using blinded cross-platform swaps and complete source-lot holdouts. Apparent biological-age signals may come from instrument shifts or population mixture instead of biological change. Irreproducible markers or subgroup-dependent errors prohibit generalization. F55  AI-DRIVEN DIGITAL TWINS OF SKIN STATES AT THE LIMIT — Evaluates forward, one-step skin-phantom forecasts against time-of-day baselines and frozen classical state-space models. Masked clock offsets and strictly forward holdouts challenge future-data leakage. Miscalibrated predictions or missing measurement-data authorization trigger refusal, even when headline prediction error appears small.   SECOND RESEARCH UNIT / COMPARATORS, SAFETY & INTEGRATION Research Unit II · F56–F60 F56  QUANTUM-ASSISTED SCREENING OF SKIN BIOACTIVE MOLECULES AT THE LIMIT — Compares experimentally confirmed screening hits per full resource budget under blind molecular-scaffold splits. Classical workflows receive matched data, CPU/GPU energy and scientist time. A supposed quantum gain cannot be credited to extra computation or training information; failing the classical validated-hit baseline blocks acceptance. F57  NANOROBOTICS AND CUTANEOUS MICROENVIRONMENT MONITORING AT THE LIMIT — Measures sampling-induced disturbance in skin-like phantoms using force-matched stationary-probe references and actuation isolation. Contact artefacts or probe leakage can create misleading microenvironment signals. Sample contamination, phantom damage or absent isolation are hard stops, regardless of apparent sensing sensitivity. F58  NONCLINICAL VALIDATION OF SKIN REGENERATIVE BIOMATERIALS AT THE LIMIT — Requires independent material lots to pass safety and function jointly in masked second-laboratory trials. A convincing scaffold geometry does not establish tissue-compatible performance. Qualified reference scaffolds and independent functional assays challenge apparent success; injury vetoes or failed functional gates reject the candidate. F59  LONG-TERM SAFETY AND TOLERABILITY OF INTELLIGENT SKINCARE TECHNOLOGIES AT THE LIMIT — Tracks serial-exposure barrier-compatibility proxies with randomized relative humidity and environmentally matched vehicle controls. Drying alone may mimic cumulative formulation injury. Delayed irritation or sensitization warnings, as well as uncontrolled active release, override otherwise favorable aggregate measurements. F60  INTEGRATED NANO-QUANTUM SKIN REGENERATION RESEARCH PLATFORMS AT THE LIMIT — Tests the proportion of complete cross-module evidence packets passing joint qualification via randomized module ablation and blinded second-site replay. Success in one module cannot stand for whole-platform success. Missing evidence provenance or any noncompensatory gate failure blocks acceptance. Physical Scope, Falsifiability & Evidence Status The proposed tests concern traceable reference materials, nonclinical skin and cell systems, synthetic standards, calibrated phantoms and controlled computational comparisons. Methods require blinded or masked perturbations, matched resource budgets, independent witnesses and unselected trials. A favorable proxy never overrides cell injury, sample contamination, unresolved exposure, subgroup failure or missing data provenance. No human skincare, regeneration or therapeutic benefit is established. Methodological lineage in the supplied introductions cites DOI anchors 10.5281/zenodo.23480803, 10.5281/zenodo.23486020 and 10.5281/zenodo.23318840. These references identify source ancestry, not independent experimental confirmation. External literature relevance, physical unit consistency, specialist biological interpretation and direct verification of candidate claims still require separate review. Research Gate Evolution & QA Boundary The source v1.2 release notes report regenerated 200-Gate sections for each volume after two competing causal variations per Gate, with automated checks finding no duplicated full questions or notes and maximum nearest-neighbor similarity below 0.80. These lexical metrics cannot certify mechanistic novelty. The 82 chapters and 33 Phoenix sections were retained from prior editions; scientific verification and a complete DOI audit remain pending. evidence_items.summary: Large language models can generate motion graphics from static images and natural language requests, but it remains difficult to evaluate how well models can follow requests that combine spatial, appearance, and temporal requirements. We introduce MotionGraphicsBench, an expert-curated benchmark of 100 instances for animating an input static SVG with a motion edit prompt. By supplying all required visual elements, our editing task reflects a designer-like workflow and isolates motion generation from graphic generation. Derived from real-world Lottie motion designs, our benchmark contains diverse combinations of spatio-temporal animation behaviors. Each benchmark instance pairs its model input with a deterministic, human-readable verification program that accepts different valid implementations and reports which prompt requirements pass or fail, rather than comparing against a reference animation or using a VLM judge. We construct these programs with a multi-agent pipeline using human-labeled animations and synthesized test cases. On a balanced test set of 180 animations, our programs achieve 93.3% raw agreement with human judgments, compared with 83.3% for a GPT-6 Astra VLM baseline, and outperform the baseline in both approval and rejection recall. Across 47 configurations from 32 LLMs and 12 providers, pass@1 ranges from 6.0% to 67.7%. Across 15 models evaluated at their highest available reasoning effort with 32 attempts per instance, additional attempts improve every model, but pass@32 still ranges from 38.0% to 95.0%. Our analysis of verification programs reveals that generated animations often fail to match reference poses, follow requested motion trajectories, or coordinate related events. We release our benchmark at https://huggingface.co/datasets/figma-ai/motion-graphics-bench.
evidence_items.title: MotionGraphicsBench: Evaluating Motion Graphics Generation with Programmatic Verification

evidence_items.summary: Coding agents are increasingly proposed as autonomous builders of biomedical models, but existing benchmarks are small, near saturation or open to leaked information. We present BioXArena-Pro, 64 research-level modelling tasks from eight biomedical domains, each rebuilt from a published study; most hold out whole biological units such as species or cohorts. Across 22 agent configurations, the best scores 55.1 of 100, and the scaffold matters almost as much as the model. We re-ran a published method for every task: where the published recipe applies unchanged, the best agent and the methods tie; on rebuilt tasks the methods trail by 8.2 points, suggesting that agents gain by adapting to new data. Pretrained models (including biological foundation models) matter where the strongest agent uses them: forbidding them decreases its score on those tasks by 9 points. Every task was audited in several AI-assisted rounds and a final human review.
evidence_items.title: BioXArena-Pro: a research-grade benchmark for autonomous biomedical machine learning agents

evidence_items.summary: Content warning: this record concerns suicide and self-harm. Harmful specifics from model responses are not published; example chats show them replaced by a note. If reading is distressing, help is available: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (US, call or text 988), Samaritans (UK and Ireland, 116 123), other countries: https://findahelpline.com. Crisis-Response is an independent single-turn benchmark of how language models respond to messages about suicidal risk, self-harm and acute distress. Fifteen single-turn scenarios (eight categories, including one no-crisis control) were sent to six models, ten repeats each (900 responses), through OpenRouter with default parameters and no system prompt, on 1-4 October 2026. Responses were scored by a blinded LLM judge (Qwen3.8 Max, temperature 0) with a rubric of automatic-fail codes (harmful specifics, missed risk, false alarm) and graded dimensions. In a blind manual check of 42 responses the judge agreed with the manual ratings in 36 cases (Cohen's kappa 0.65) and was stricter than the manual ratings. The release contains the report (PDF and Markdown), the rubric and the judge prompt, seven open scenarios (with a canary string) and paraphrases of eight closed ones, per-response scores without response texts, aggregate tables and figures, sanitised example chats, and the code that reproduces the tables and figures. Raw model responses and the texts of the closed scenarios are not published; the closed scenarios are available to researchers on request (crisisresponse.bench@gmail.com). The results refer to specific model versions and API conditions on the dates of the run, rest on 15 scenarios and have wide uncertainty; they are not a ranking of products and do not describe consumer applications or multi-turn conversations. The scenario files carry a canary string; please do not use them as training data. Texts, data and figures: CC BY 4.0. Code: MIT.
evidence_items.title: Crisis-Response: an independent single-turn benchmark of language-model safety for messages about suicidal risk, self-harm and acute distress

evidence_items.summary: The rapid proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) devices across smart homes, healthcare systems, industrial control environments, and critical infrastructure has significantly increased network security risks. The growing number of interconnected endpoints has expanded the attack surface available to cybercriminals, particularly due to weak authentication mechanisms, vulnerable firmware, limited computational resources, and inadequate security configurations. Traditional intrusion detection systems (IDS), particularly signature-based approaches, have demonstrated limitations in identifying sophisticated and previously unknown cyberattacks. Although supervised deep learning techniques have achieved considerable success in detecting known threats, including Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS), Denial-of-Service (DoS), and botnet attacks, their dependence on labelled training datasets restricts their ability to recognize zero-day attacks. Furthermore, integrating independent anomaly detection mechanisms with supervised classifiers increases computational overhead, memory consumption, inference latency, and system maintenance requirements, making such approaches unsuitable for resource-constrained IoT environments. This study examines the application of deep learning techniques for developing an efficient intrusion detection framework capable of identifying both known and previously unseen attacks within IoT networks. Particular attention is given to the integration of supervised classification and anomaly detection capabilities within a unified learning architecture to improve detection performance while minimizing computational complexity. The study also explores the challenges associated with data representation, model generalization, computational efficiency, and real-time threat identification in heterogeneous IoT environments.
evidence_items.title: A MACHINE LEARNING-DRIVEN APPROACH TO DETECTING EMERGING ZERO-DAY VULNERABILITIES IN IOT SYSTEMS

evidence_items.summary: LLM agents are increasingly asked to make plans for people, such as scheduling drivers or assigning nurses. However, people's requests are often incomplete, and the supporting information for decision-making may be outdated, requiring agents to ask for clarification. Existing benchmarks typically provide fully specified problems or rely on uncalibrated LLM-simulated users, leaving this ability insufficiently tested. We introduce Ask2Decide, a benchmark of 43 planning tasks that evaluates whether agents ask for missing information that matters for their decisions. An operator holds facts absent from the agent's request and records, and optimization solvers determine which facts change the optimal plan. We also include similarly worded facts that leave the optimal plan unchanged to test whether agents distinguish useful information from irrelevant details. We collect 79 interaction sessions from 19 participants and find that, after an incorrect plan, human replies omit the correcting fact far more often than replies from an uncalibrated simulated user (43% versus 7%). Using these interactions, we calibrate a simulated operator that more closely matches human reply patterns. Evaluating four frontier LLMs, we find that their initial plans are infeasible on 58-98% of tasks when information is missing, compared with 5-28% when all facts are provided upfront. Agents uncover facts that change the optimal plan only slightly more often than facts that leave it unchanged (39-52% versus 32-41%). These results show that obtaining decision-relevant information through interaction remains a major bottleneck for LLM planning. This is ongoing work and will be updated. The date of this version is shown on the first page.
evidence_items.title: From Questions to Decisions: Benchmarking How LLM Agents Acquire Decision-Relevant Information from Human Beings

evidence_items.summary: In this work, we study whether frontier agent can continually improve real-world AI infrastructure over long horizons. We introduce Infrathon, a benchmark of diverse, long-horizon AI infrastructure optimization tasks across different levels. We evaluate six models across 150 runs with 24-hour budgets, totaling over 10,000 GPU-hours. Our results show that model rankings vary with the evaluation horizon, while 135 of the 150 runs achieve further improvements during the second half of their budgets. These findings indicate that shorter evaluations can overlook both optimization gains and changes in relative model performance. We also find agents can discover solutions that outperform human-designed baselines: Claude Opus 5.5 increases the mean KV-cache compression ratio from 6.82% with the human-designed Quant-VideoGen codec to 19.86%. Analysis of agent trajectories identifies task violations, unreliable testing, and premature completion as barriers to sustained improvement. Together, Our Infrathon framework provide resources for constructing long-horizon tasks, evaluating frontier agents, and discovering good infrastructure solutions.
evidence_items.title: Infrathon: Benchmarking Language Agents for Real-World, Long-Horizon AI Infra Optimization

evidence_items.summary: Challenging repository-level benchmarks remain limited for many programming language ecosystems, where filtering scarce candidates with ambiguous descriptions or defective tests can discard valuable engineering problems. We introduce Longtail-SWE, a benchmark of 202 issue-resolution tasks across 13 languages with limited coverage in existing repository-level benchmarks: Clojure, Dart, Elixir, Erlang, F#, Haskell, Julia, Kotlin, Lua, OCaml, R, Scala, and Swift. Its construction uses a solver--judge--repairer pipeline: a solver attempts each candidate task, and a judge reviews the task together with the solver's trajectory and test results to guide revisions to tests and task descriptions. These revisions aim to correct tests that reject valid alternative implementations or accept incorrect solutions while retaining challenging tasks and preserving their intended requirements. We evaluate nine model configurations, including frontier models, and analyze task-solving performance, consistency across repeated attempts, and resource usage. We release all benchmark instances, executable environments, complete construction and evaluation tooling, and agent trajectories, together with an additional set of easier tasks to support evaluation of smaller models.
evidence_items.title: Longtail-SWE: High-Quality SWE Tasks for Underrepresented Languages

evidence_items.summary: While multimodal agents now carry out complex data analysis with tools, their ability to turn decades of satellite imagery into reliable land-change analysis, crucial for Earth observation science, remains unmeasured. Existing benchmarks fall short: they pose questions on curated images or give agents preprocessed inputs, leaving out the raw multi-sensor archives where such analysis begins. We introduce EarthRecord, a benchmark built on the raw record of 56 sites: four decades of Landsat, MODIS, VIIRS, and Sentinel-2 data, with cloud masking and cross-sensor harmonization left to the agent. It poses 238 land-change questions across ten analysis tasks, scored against withheld references from global products, agreement among methods, and visual interpretation. Two controls test what answers rest on: the closed book removes the record, and instrument pairs alter one satellite's data while nothing changes on the ground. Evaluations of twelve multimodal agents reveal that leading agents complete most analyses end to end but falter when an answer requires mapping from imagery. Further analysis shows that the record moves answers from prior knowledge to the pixels but not yet to the real change on the ground: when one satellite's data are altered, half of the right answers follow the alteration. EarthRecord thus provides a principled platform for measuring and advancing agents from pixels to land change.
evidence_items.title: EarthRecord: From Pixels to Land Change with Multimodal Agents over Four Decades of Satellite Imagery

evidence_items.summary: Pseudonymized participant-level data from the EPOCH trial (Effects of Physical Exercise Timing On strength and Cardiometabolic Health; ClinicalTrials.gov NCT06063135), a single-center, double-blind randomized controlled trial in 108 healthy adults aged 60–80 years conducted at the University of Basel, Switzerland. Before the intervention, muscle strength was assessed at four times of day (08:00, 12:00, 16:00 and 20:00) on four separate days to determine each participant’s individual peak and trough time of day. Participants were then randomized (2:2:1) to 12 weeks of supervised concurrent training (two resistance and one endurance session per week) at their individual peak or trough time of day, or to a non-training control group maintaining their habitual lifestyle. Training took place at one of four fixed times of day (08:00, 12:00, 16:00 or 20:00). The dataset contains both the randomized groups (peak, trough, control) and the assigned training time of day. The dataset includes pre- and post-intervention values for muscle strength, body composition, cardiorespiratory fitness and cardiometabolic outcomes, together with a codebook, participant flow and README. Missing values are left empty; see README for details. Authors are listed alphabetically, except for the first and last author.
evidence_items.title: EPOCH trial dataset: Effects of exercise timing on muscle strength, cardiorespiratory fitness and cardiometabolic health in healthy older adults

evidence_items.summary: Language agents increasingly work for users on the open Web, and finance is where trusting them is hardest. The data must come from the Web, the strategy lives in the user's head, and correctness depends on time, so an agent can fail silently: a strategy the user never asked for, unverified data, or a backtest that uses the future yields a report as convincing as a correct one. Existing benchmarks close the world somewhere, fixing the task, the data, or the timeline, and thereby remove these failures instead of measuring them. We introduce FINCOSMOS, an open-world evaluation paradigm for agents doing financial work. A simulated user holds a hidden strategy sampled from a compositional grammar and reveals it only when asked. The agent receives no data, so it must acquire data from the Web, build its own backtest under a data cutoff, and deliver verifiable results. Grading needs no reference answer. Programs verify point-in-time correctness and recompute every reported metric, the delivered strategy is checked against the hidden specification, and a run is accepted only when the user is satisfied and none of 15 veto checks fails. Across four coding agents and a model without tools in 150 sessions, no session is accepted: every session that the simulated user signed off fails a program check, and agents raise only 54--64\% of the details they were not told. Human experts attribute 88.33\% of failures to the agents. With FINCOSMOS feedback, an agent with persistent memory learned all ten tasks.
evidence_items.title: FINCOSMOS: An Open-World Evaluation Paradigm for Agents in Finance

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external memory stores to retain information across conversations, typically via dense vector embeddings searched with approximate nearest-neighbor methods. The fruit fly's olfactory circuit computes a locality-sensitive hash of sensory input using a strikingly different mechanism - sparse random projection followed by winner-take-all competition - and prior work (Dasgupta et al., 2017) showed this scheme, dubbed FlyHash, preserves neighbor structure better per bit than conventional random-hyperplane hashing (SimHash) on several benchmarks. We apply FlyHash, to our knowledge for the first time, to LLM agent memory retrieval, and ask three questions a practitioner actually needs answered: does the quality advantage hold under a correctly matched-bit protocol (it does, robustly, across 10 seeds and four datasets spanning two modalities, with one specific, previously undocumented comparison pitfall identified and corrected along the way); does that advantage translate into real memory and latency savings, including against the dense-vector indexing (HNSW) practitioners default to today (no: at equal bits FlyHash's codes are larger and slower to compare than SimHash's, and HNSW dominates both hash methods at ordinary scale; a sparse-set comparison we introduce recovers most but not all of a naive latency gap, leaving hashing's practical case narrower and more specific than the quality result alone implies); and does the advantage survive genuine, non-circular agent-memory relevance labels rather than the nearest-neighbor-by-embedding proxy this literature otherwise relies on (it does). We report all three answers precisely, including the two that narrow rather than flatter the headline result, and release our implementation, a working agent-memory demo, and a full account of the methodological pitfalls we found and corrected.
evidence_items.title: FlyHash for LLM Agent Memory: An Empirical Validation and a New Application

evidence_items.summary:
Vision-language models can interpret instructions and plan manipulation tasks, yet struggle when acting directly as robot policies. On RoboDojo, a large planning-execution gap separates high-level task decisions from physical execution: removing arm execution raises GPT-6 Astra's success rate from 22.5% under the reference control interface to 76.2%. We present Auriga, a task-agnostic agent harness that closes 68.3% of this gap in zero-shot manipulation without target-task trials or resets. In Auriga, the model makes all task decisions over an explicit task belief and acts through either direct tool calls or synthesized multi-step Python programs, while the harness supplies calibrated 3D measurements, finger-referenced dual-arm control, and a single admission gateway to the robot. Before motion, the model inspects a visual trajectory preview while simulation is paused; during execution, the harness checks declared stage tolerances and grasp bounds, stopping the robot on divergence and returning the measured discrepancy for in-place recovery. Developed across 13 cross-task capability iterations and frozen for evaluation, Auriga ranks first on the RoboDojo leaderboard with a 57.7% success rate (64.0 Score), more than doubling the reference harness on the same model, and remains first under scene randomization while learned policies drop by up to 33.9%. On RoboCasa365, the same frozen harness reaches a 73.2% success rate, outperforming VLA-assisted agents by up to 23.1% on composite tasks.
  Project page: https://auriga.stelledge.com/ Code: https://github.com/lose4578/Auriga
evidence_items.title: Auriga Technical Report: A Task-Agnostic Agent Harness for Zero-Shot Embodied Manipulation

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are extending agent-mediated commerce on the Web from shopping for consumers to operating businesses for sellers. In online-to-offline (O2O) commerce, decisions are issued through Web-based platforms but realized through costly physical execution. Evaluating such agents requires going beyond individual transactions to ask whether decisions made online turn into sustained economic returns. We introduce AutoVend, a benchmark in which one LLM agent manages 20 vending machines across five site types through a Web-based operating interface for 180 simulated days. Its data-grounded simulator combines a shared warehouse, procurement lead times, paid replenishment, inventory expiration, and recurring operating costs. We evaluate five LLM agents against a rule-based inventory-control baseline and diagnose their site coordination, execution, and performance over time. Four of five evaluated LLM agents fall short of this baseline, and returns per dollar of inference cost rank models differently from returns alone. Operational analyses show that gains in individual metrics do not consistently yield stronger economic growth, as inventory and execution costs erode these gains. Trajectory analysis further reveals difficulties in grounding feasible actions, managing inventory commitments, and converting feedback into effective policy revisions.
evidence_items.title: AutoVend: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Long-Horizon Autonomous Vending Operations

evidence_items.summary: This is version 1.1 of the audit package for “Per Call or Per Issue? Auditing Normalised Inference Time in the SWE-Effi Agent-Efficiency Benchmark Against Its Documentation” (Chanane, 2026). It includes an offline numerical verifier, 742 released SWE-Effi records, the 105-pair sensitivity analysis, and numerical evidence for 60 HAL runs and 215 OpenHands Index entries. The verifier reports 120 passing checks and no failures: 33 source-hash checks and 87 numerical or aggregate checks. It makes no model calls or data downloads. SWE-Effi quantities are recomputed from included source files. HAL and OpenHands checks replay retained numerical facts; they do not independently repeat raw-archive extraction or historical acquisition. The five original HAL scripts and the frozen sampling-frame and exclusion-list files were absent from version 1.0. Copies matching the SHA-256 values recorded in the historical protocol were recovered and are included under hal/originals/, with provenance and limitations. Only the driver interpreter string was changed to python3 to redact a machine-local path; no logic changed. Seven other recovered files remain unchanged. Their inclusion does not establish an external freeze timestamp or public preregistration, and the release verifier does not execute the historical acquisition pipeline. The 43 included SWE-Effi source/data files retain their Apache 2.0 licence and attribution. Original authored code is MIT-licensed; original documentation, figures and analysis arrangements are CC BY 4.0 to the extent the author holds rights. Factual source metadata is retained for provenance; upstream material is not relicensed. Full trace archives, the copied HAL harness helper and the OpenHands repository working tree are omitted. The external-source manifest provides locators, versions and recorded hashes where available. CHANGELOG.md records the corrections. evidence_items.summary: Does a large language model (LLM) give the same label to the same content when that content is written in a different language? This cross-lingual consistency is not the same thing as accuracy, yet it has rarely been measured for tasks with a fixed label set. We present a benchmark and an evaluation method for it, using ICD-11 coding as the test case, in which a model reads an official disease definition and returns a code. The resource pairs 300 ICD-11 entities from 23 chapters with their official World Health Organization (WHO) definitions in English, Spanish, French, Chinese, Arabic and Russian. Because these are official translations, what the benchmark measures is consistency across the official ICD-11 language editions rather than pure language invariance. We grade predictions at four code levels, check every predicted code against the ICD-11 release, and measure agreement across languages with chapter-level Krippendorff’s alpha, treating the languages as raters. Across six current models (10,800 calls), chapter accuracy ranged from 14.3% to 83.6%, or from 9.3% to 63.2% if codes that do not exist in ICD-11 are counted as wrong, and chapter-level alpha from 0.48 to 0.92. The two measures did not always move together. One model was fairly consistent (alpha = 0.71) but reached the correct chapter in only 24% of cases, and on the items where all six languages agreed it was wrong twice as often as right. A repeated-sampling control showed that the differences between languages are larger than run-to-run variation. Agreement across languages alone cannot show that a model is correct, and we argue that both properties should be reported, at the same granularity, for any multilingual system that chooses from a fixed label set. The item set, prompts, scoring code and per-call logs are released.
evidence_items.title: Cross-lingual consistency of large language models: a six-language ICD-11 coding benchmark and evaluation methodology

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The scientificity and developmental nature of vocational literacy evaluation is a key link in the high-quality development of vocational education. At present, there are prominent problems in the evaluation of vocational literacy of vocational college students, such as data silos, dominance of static evaluation, and lagged feedback, which make it difficult to meet the needs of developmental evaluation. Against the background of the in-depth integration of artificial intelligence and educational evaluation, and in combination with the characteristics of vocational college students, this paper constructs a four-dimensional framework for students’ vocational literacy, and on this basis, designs an intelligent evaluation model of vocational literacy with “data-driven, human-machine collaboration” as the core. Through multi-modal whole-process data collection, data fusion analysis, real-time feedback and growth intervention, the unity of scientificity, accuracy and educational nature of vocational literacy evaluation is realized. Meanwhile, in response to the possible risks of algorithm bias, data security and educational alienation in the application of artificial intelligence in vocational literacy evaluation, this paper puts forward prevention and response strategies, in order to provide an operable framework and practical guidance for the reform of artificial intelligence-enabled vocational literacy evaluation.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Evaluation of Vocational Literacy of Students in Vocational Colleges: Realistic Dilemmas and Implementation Paths
