evidence_items.summary: BACKGROUND: Many transfusion reactions are not reported to hemovigilance systems, and the features needed to recognize them are often documented only in free-text clinical notes. We sought to develop and evaluate an open-source, multi-agent artificial intelligence (AI) pipeline to extract transfusion reaction features defined by the National Healthcare Safety Network (NHSN) Hemovigilance Module from clinical notes. METHODS: We curated 181 features from the NHSN protocol and developed a multi-stage pipeline that extracted features, their timing, and clinical details from free-text notes. Three open-weight large language models (Qwen 3.6-27B, GPT-OSS-120B, and Kimi K3) were applied to 50 notes from expert-written scenarios, published case reports, and MIMIC-IV discharge summaries. Two physicians independently evaluated every model output in a blinded interface. The primary analysis was restricted to feature occurrences with concordant physician assessments. RESULTS: Physicians agreed on 1,201 of 1,343 co-rated feature occurrences (89.4%; Krippendorff's alpha 0.73). Precision was above 0.98 for all models. Sensitivity was 0.774 (95% CI 0.745-0.800) for Kimi K3, 0.636 (0.604-0.667) for GPT-OSS-120B, and 0.624 (0.593-0.655) for Qwen 3.6-27B, and specificity ranged from 0.952 to 0.991. Omissions accounted for more than 94% of false negatives. Timing and clinical details were judged supported or reasonable in more than 92% and 97% of assessments, respectively. Results were consistent across note sources and in analyses including discordant assessments. CONCLUSION: Multi-agent AI pipelines provide a feasible method for extracting transfusion reaction signals from clinical notes with high precision. Our work may have applications in active hemovigilance, reaction classification, and big data research.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract We evaluate the released Aurora 0.4-degree Air Pollution checkpoint against CAMS, persistence, and hourly background-station observations for 96 initializations spanning 2024. Against CAMS, Aurora reduces mean squared error relative to persistence by 38.1-42.6% for PM2.5 and 49.1-52.3% for PM10. At sampled station times, its mean absolute error is lower than that of the benchmark-selected CAMS fields in all six combinations of three regions and two pollutants; 95% initialization-date bootstrap intervals exclude zero. At +12 h, 6.27% of global PM2.5 and 7.84% of PM10 grid-point values are negative, whereas matched CAMS states are non-negative; subsequent forecast steps use positivity clamping. The evaluated outputs provide no forecast distribution. Perturbing four static source-related inputs produces small, nearly additive regional responses, whose relationship to changes in actual emissions remains untested. Observational agreement, physical constraints, and input sensitivity thus yield distinct assessments of the same forecasts.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract We examine supervised classification of stars, galaxies, and quasars using a 100,000-object catalogue distributed as the Stellar Classification Dataset (SDSS17). The final input vector contains five optical magnitudes and spectroscopic redshift. We develop the mathematical connection between broadband measurements, thermal radiation, colour indices, and wavelength shifts, then formulate the classification problem through posterior probabilities, empirical risk, decision-tree impurity, and ensemble prediction. The saved project notebook compares logistic regression, a decision tree, random forest, and XGBoost on one stratified 80/20 train–test split. Random forest has the highest recorded accuracy, 0.97970, corresponding to 406 errors among 20,000 test objects, whereas XGBoost has the highest macro one-versus-rest ROC-AUC, 0.995771. An independent exploratory forest assigns 0.638909 of its normalised impurity importance to redshift. We derive the identity between support-weighted recall and accuracy, establish the information-preserving role of a colour-plus-anchor transformation, and explain why an additional measurement can improve Bayes-optimal prediction without guaranteeing improvement for a finite fitted model. These are standard analytical results used to interpret the experiment, rather than claims of a new learning algorithm. The evidence supports an internal catalogue benchmark, not demonstrated photometry-only inference or transfer to another survey. Results come from recorded notebook outputs; the original CSV, fitted estimators, and object-level predictions were unavailable for independent rerunning and further empirical validation.
evidence_items.title: Intelligent Identification of Astronomical Objects: a physics-motivated benchmark of supervised classification

evidence_items.summary: Porinaceae is one of the most common families of foliicolous lichens in tropical regions. Despite its abundance, major gaps remain in our understanding of its diversity and phylogeny. This study addresses these knowledge gaps and examines photobiont selectivity in Madagascar and the Indian Ocean Islands. In total, 114 lichen specimens from Madagascar and the neighbouring islands of Mauritius and Mayotte were sequenced. Mycobiont diversity was investigated using the mtSSU and ITS regions, while photobiont diversity and selectivity were assessed using the rbc L marker. Phenotypic traits, including ascospore and perithecial characteristics, were evaluated alongside molecular data to support species delimitation. Thirty-seven Porinaceae taxa were recognised using an integrative taxonomic approach, including six species newly described here: Porina cincta Debaene & Ertz, P. complanata Debaene & Ertz, P. madagascariensis Debaene & Ertz, P. mayottensis Debaene & Ertz, P. parva Debaene, Diederich & Ertz, and P. trichocoronata Debaene & Ertz. The rbc L data recovered 25 algal haplotypes distributed across six major clades, four of which were newly recovered. Despite limited morphological differentiation, the mycobiont exhibited unexpectedly high genetic diversity, and some traditionally diagnostic characters, such as ascospore septation, proved to be unreliable at times. These patterns were accompanied by strong phylogeographic structuring and high levels of island endemism. Bipartite network analyses revealed complex symbiotic interactions, with both highly specific and more flexible mycobiont-photobiont associations, alongside substantial photobiont diversity. Altogether, this study emphasises the need for extensive DNA multilocus sampling and type-linked material, combined with thorough phenotypic assessments, to refine species and genus concepts within Porinaceae .
evidence_items.title: Integrative taxonomy reveals hidden fungal and algal diversity in foliicolous Porinaceae (Ascomycota, Ostropales) from Madagascar and the Indian Ocean Islands

evidence_items.summary: Deoxynivalenol (DON) can enter cereal-derived beverages through contaminated ingredients, yet RNA measurements do not quantify toxin burden. We reanalyzed eight public barley, wheat, and Fusarium graminearum transcriptomic series while retaining each study’s design. The analysis included 251 sample-level profiles plus public comparison-level fungal data. At 48 h in barley, eight of 344 eligible Gene Ontology pathways passed discovery-stage bidirectional rules; all eight happened to be upward. Three pathways, including glutathione and aromatic amino acid metabolism, had both purified-DON-associated and infection-associated support, whereas five represented broader infection responses. Seven non-phenylpropanoid pathways remained upward across all 77 pathway-by-contrast tests after limiting each barley gene to one wheat ortholog, although 72 retained false-discovery-rate (FDR) support. In the original exploratory gene screen, eight barley–wheat ortholog pairs were positive across studies; six remained after applying BH FDR < 0.05 to the direct-DON component, and five were also homeolog-concordant. A later barley chemotype dataset yielded no FDR-significant eligible pathway, but its cultivar, chemotype, time, mapping coverage, and sample size limit interpretation. Fungal TRI-cluster transcription increased after FgSfp1 deletion, whereas the source study separately reported 95.4% lower DON yield. This directional comparison was not a matched transcript-toxin calibration. Host pathways and fungal TRI RNA describe context-dependent biological states, not chemical DON concentration. Their possible beverage relevance is limited to upstream hypothesis generation and prioritization of chemical testing.
evidence_items.title: Context-dependent cereal defense and the limits of TRI-cluster transcription as a proxy for deoxynivalenol: A cross-study transcriptomic analysis

evidence_items.summary: Automated classification of rice seeds is essential for quality assessment and sorting in modern agriculture. This paper presents a comprehensive study on rice seed classification utilizing deep learning techniques, particularly Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). We reviewed existing research and proposed three CNN architectures: Model1 - A basic CNN architecture; Model2 - Integrating transfer learning with MobileNetV2, and Model3 - An advanced version with additional optimization techniques. A novel dataset including 5000 rice seed images from diverse sources was utilized. Pre-processing techniques, including image cropping and resizing, ensured uniform input dimensions for CNN models. Experimental results illustrate the efficacy of the proposed models. Model3 - Incorporating various optimization techniques, achieved a peak accuracy of 95%, surpassing its predecessors. Comparative analysis revealed Model3's higher accuracy, recall, and accuracy scores, highlighting its robustness in accurately classifying rice seed varieties. In conclusion, this study emphasizes the significance of deep learning techniques in rice seed classification, offering promising solutions for automating seed quality assessment and enhancing agricultural practices.
evidence_items.title: Deep learning paradigms for rice seed classification: a comparative study and novel architectures

evidence_items.summary: Background: Acute myeloid leukaemia (AML) is a haematological malignancy that can involve extramedullary tissues, including the orbit and ocular structures. Orbital leukemic infiltration is an uncommon but potentially vision-threatening manifestation, particularly in paediatric patients. Case Presentation: A 13-year-old male with a known history of acute myeloid leukaemia presented with gradually progressive swelling of the eyelids in both eyes over eight months. The patient had previously received four doses of chemotherapy and radiation therapy and was undergoing oral metronomic treatment. Ophthalmological examination revealed severely reduced visual acuity, limited to hand movement perception (HM+) in both eyes. Anterior segment examination documented bilateral localized anterior staphyloma. B-scan ultrasonography revealed vitreous echoes, structural ocular changes, and orbital findings suggestive of leukemic infiltration. Flash visual evoked potential testing was also performed to assess visual pathway function. Diagnosis: Based on the clinical history, ophthalmological examination, and ultrasonographic findings, bilateral orbital leukemic involvement was clinically assessed in association with localized anterior staphyloma. Management and Outcome: The patient underwent multidisciplinary ophthalmological evaluation, including recommendations for oculoplastic and corneal consultations. A guarded visual prognosis was explained, and further ocular surgical intervention was considered in relation to the patient's systemic condition. Subsequent treatment response and visual outcome were not documented in the available records. Conclusion: This case highlights the importance of comprehensive ophthalmic evaluation in children with acute myeloid leukemia presenting with persistent eyelid swelling and severe visual impairment.
evidence_items.title: Bilateral Orbital Involvement with Severe Visual Impairment and Anterior Staphyloma in a 13-year-old boy with Acute Myeloid Leukaemia: A Case Report

evidence_items.summary: Dataset overview This dataset provides quality-controlled, provenance-aware derived hydrological and suspended-sediment monitoring indicators for five stations in the Upper Danube and Rába River system in northwestern Hungary, covering observations from 2007 to 2026. The source compilation comprises 840 measurement records from irregular field campaigns. The released data product contains: 61 station–year monitoring and data-coverage records; 76 grouped, quality-screened hydrological and sediment-variable distributions; station-level quality-control and laboratory-linkage indicators; standardized metadata, a data dictionary, reproducible Python code and seven scientific figures. The monitoring stations are Rába–Árpás, Rába–Győr, Rába–Kenyeri, Danube–Vámosszabadi and Danube–Nagybajcs. The Rába–Kenyeri extension incorporates 64 distinct discharge measurement events spanning 2014, 2018 and 2020–2026. No verified suspended-sediment concentration observations are available for Kenyeri in the integrated records. Data processing and quality assurance The dataset distinguishes observed measurements from derived statistical indicators. Quality assurance includes completeness and duplicate checks, source reconciliation, measurement-unit assessment, arithmetic consistency screening and documentation of uncertain records. Numerical distribution indicators are released only for groups containing at least 12 eligible observations. Reported quantiles are rounded to two significant digits. The released indicators describe irregularly sampled measurement campaigns and must not be interpreted as continuous daily hydrological series or direct annual sediment-yield estimates.
evidence_items.title: Quality-aware derived hydrological and suspended-sediment monitoring indicators for the Upper Danube and Rába River system (2007–2026)

evidence_items.summary: Digital Twin (DT) technology and Artificial Intelligence (AI) are increasingly recognized as transformative technologies for improving agricultural land assessment, monitoring, and productivity management. Digital Twins facilitate high-frequency data exchange and synchronization between physical agricultural environments and their virtual representations, enabling continuous monitoring, predictive analysis, and informed decision-making. This study examines the integration of Digital Twin technology and Artificial Intelligence techniques for predictive modeling of agricultural land performance. The proposed approach considers the application of Internet of Things (IoT) devices, remote sensing, Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS), machine learning algorithms, and agricultural data analytics to evaluate and predict important land performance indicators. These indicators include soil fertility, moisture availability, climatic conditions, vegetation characteristics, land suitability, and crop productivity. By integrating real-time environmental observations with intelligent computational models, the framework provides opportunities to identify productivity constraints, forecast changes in agricultural land conditions, and support efficient resource allocation. The study further considers the challenges affecting the adoption of advanced digital agricultural technologies, particularly high implementation costs, extended investment recovery periods, limited technical expertise, inadequate field data, infrastructural deficiencies, and the relatively low adoption of precision agriculture technologies among smallholder farmers. The integration of Digital Twins and AI offers significant potential for improving agricultural forecasting, strengthening land management decisions, and promoting sustainable agricultural development.
evidence_items.title: INTEGRATING DIGITAL TWIN TECHNOLOGY AND ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE FOR PREDICTIVE MODELING OF AGRICULTURAL LAND PRODUCTIVITY

evidence_items.summary: Integrated Approach Towards Management of Thyroid Disorders and Poly-Endocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS): A Research-Based Clinical Yogatherapy Module   Background: Thyroid Disorders and Poly-Endocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS) are common endocrine disorders associated with metabolic, reproductive, psychological, and cardiovascular complications. Hypothyroidism is characterised by fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation, depression, and menstrual disturbances, while PMOS is associated with insulin resistance, hyperandrogenism, obesity, menstrual irregularities, infertility, acne, hirsutism, and reduced quality of life. The coexistence of these disorders may further aggravate metabolic dysfunction and endocrine imbalance. Growing scientific evidence suggests that Yoga Therapy and integrative lifestyle interventions may provide significant benefits in disease management by improving hormonal regulation, metabolic health, and psychological well-being. Objective : The present study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of an Integrated Therapeutic Approach combining Clinical Yoga Therapy, Lifestyle Medicine, Traditional Herbal Medicine, Homoeopathic Medicine, and evidence-based supportive supplementation in the management of Thyroid Disorders and PMOS. Methods : A 12-week integrated intervention programme was implemented among participants aged 18–55 years diagnosed with thyroid disorders and/or PMOS. The intervention consisted of Clinical Yoga Therapy sessions conducted five days per week, including Sukshma Vyayama, therapeutic asanas, pranayama, relaxation techniques, Yoga Nidra, and meditation. Lifestyle Medicine components included nutritional counselling, physical activity promotion, sleep optimization, stress management, behavioural modification, and psycho-social support.
evidence_items.title: Integrated Approach Towards Management of Thyroid Disorders  and Poly-Endocrine Metabolic Ovarian Syndrome (PMOS): A Research-Based Clinical Yoga Therapy Module

evidence_items.summary: The increasing adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) technologies has transformed information service delivery in academic libraries, creating new opportunities for improving reference services, information retrieval, and scholarly communication. Academic libraries in South-South Nigeria are gradually embracing AI-powered applications to complement librarians' professional expertise and respond to the evolving information needs of students, researchers, and academic staff. This study examines human–artificial intelligence integration in reference services delivery in academic libraries, with particular attention to the application of AI-supported tools such as Grammarly and QuillBot. It explores how these technologies support citation generation, reference formatting, grammatical correction, information organization, and other academic information services. The study further considers the complementary roles of librarians and AI applications in improving service efficiency, accessibility, accuracy, and user satisfaction. Human expertise remains essential in evaluating information credibility, interpreting complex research enquiries, providing personalized guidance, and ensuring compliance with academic referencing standards. However, the integration of AI into reference services also presents challenges relating to technological infrastructure, digital literacy, inaccurate AI-generated information, data privacy, ethical concerns, and institutional readiness. The study highlights the importance of developing appropriate AI integration strategies that combine technological capabilities with professional librarianship practices. It emphasizes continuous staff training, adequate technological infrastructure, institutional policies, and responsible AI utilization as essential requirements for sustainable implementation.
evidence_items.title: Integrating Human Intelligence and Artificial Intelligence in Reference Services Delivery in Academic Libraries in South-South Nigeria

evidence_items.summary: The increasing availability of judicial decisions in digital form creates important opportunities for legal research and public access, while simultaneously raising concerns regarding the disclosure of personal and sensitive information. This work investigates the automated anonymization of court decisions using transformer-based Named Entity Recognition (NER). An NER-based anonymization pipeline is applied to 107 decisions from the Kansas Court of Appeals obtained through the Caselaw Access Project, while a manually annotated subset of 21 decisions is used for quantitative evaluation. The analysis focuses on three entity categories: PERSON, ORGANIZATION, and LOCATION. The evaluated BERT-based NER model achieves F1-scores of 88.93%, 81.06%, and 96.83%, respectively. The results reveal substantially different precision–recall characteristics across entity types, with missed personal names representing the most important privacy-related errors and organization detection exhibiting a tendency toward over-anonymization. Qualitative analysis further identifies problems involving compound entity fragmentation, ambiguous names, and inconsistent treatment of repeated references. The findings demonstrate that entity-specific evaluation is essential for assessing judicial anonymization systems, since recognition errors have different implications for privacy protection and document utility.
evidence_items.title: GENEDIS 2026 – Paper [106] – [Automated Anonymization of Court Decisions Using Transformer-Based Named Entity Recognition]

evidence_items.summary: Why might households hesitate to bring a humanoid robot home? This exploratory, pre-adoption study identifies four acceptance issues for home humanoid robots (form, safety, trust and privacy) and the key technical and governance challenges they imply. Data and method. Using one product case, 1X NEO, the study derives the issues from 16 expert evaluation texts (Feb 2025–Jul 2026) and 827 online comments from Hacker News and Reddit (Feb 2024–May 2026). It then reads them through the domestication model (Silverstone, Hirsch & Morley, 1992) and published household studies of existing devices such as robot vacuums, smart speakers and shared computers. Argument. Each issue marks a point where the judgments and adjustments households already make with existing devices stop working for a humanoid. Examples are giving a device a place and role, controlling access by placement, widening what is entrusted through use, and covering or switching a device off. Responses should therefore move from improving specifications to enabling household judgment and adjustment. In the deck this means four shifts: from physical form to temporal form, from physical safety to perceived safety, from single-task reliability to calibrated trust and trust repair, and from owner consent to bystander privacy. Challenges. The deck sets out representative technical challenges with reported levels and first-stage targets, covering response latency, stopping time, uncertainty-aware help-seeking and device security. It then links these to design, validation and governance measures that support household judgment. Scope. Data were collected before customer deliveries. Figures from experimental settings are reference points, not product measurements. The views expressed are the author’s own and do not represent ETRI.
evidence_items.title: Acceptance Issues and Key Challenges for Home Humanoid Robots

evidence_items.summary: Myalgic Encephalomyelitis/Chronic Fatigue Syndrome (ME/CFS) is a chronic illness characterized by debilitating, heterogeneous symptoms and variable outcomes. Prognostic tools remain scarce in a diagnosis-weighted field. This study examines whether multidimensional baseline patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs), analysed with explainable machine learning, can predict heterogeneous 12-month outcomes and reveal outcome structure under burden, discordance, imbalance, missingness, and non-linearity. Secondary analysis used a UK specialist-service cohort with baseline and 12-month data (n = 438). PROMs captured symptom-functional domains, while follow-up PROMs and Clinical Global Impression scales derived continuous fatigue change, improved versus worsened trajectories, and multi-pattern classifications. Regression, ensembles, support vector machines, PCA, clustering, partial dependence, and SHAP were evaluated using cross-validation, calibration, discrimination, error metrics, and decision analysis. Models explained continuous fatigue change variance and distinguished trajectories. Functional disability, daytime sleepiness, pain, and fatigue predicted deterioration; improvement remained weak and unstable. Clustering identified severity subgroups, not prognostic classes. Random forests balanced discrimination, calibration, and clinical benefit for meaningful deterioration-risk identification. Findings suggest deterioration is machine-detectable whereas recovery resists prediction, supporting structural outcome fragmentation. Recovery was not worsening’s inverse; domains decoupled over time. PROM-based machine learning may support early warning of deterioration. Future work should prioritize validation, multimodal integration, and fragmentation-aware prognostic frameworks.

evidence_items.summary: As AI agents become increasingly capable, users must still recognize when and how to ask for help, leaving many opportunities for useful support unrealized. Proactive agents hold the promise to close this gap, but effective proactivity requires understanding users' real-time activities and personalizing intervention timing so that assistance is offered when it is likely to be helpful rather than disruptive. We introduce deep personalization, a closed-loop process that connects continuous context observation with continual agent adaptation: an agent observes user activity, selectively retains long-term context, and adapts intervention decisions from implicit feedback. We initiate deep personalization in Coco, a proactive desktop agent, by having a separate Observer Agent that monitors desktop activity, maintains compact long-term user modeling context, and learns when assistance is desirable from implicit signals such as engagement, dismissal, explicit requests, and repeated work patterns. We further develop efficient on-device strategies to enable the Observer Agent to run on local AI compute platforms without streaming raw activity data off-device. For evaluation at scale without collecting sensitive real-user activity, we introduce a data-synthesis pipeline that transforms existing computer-use trajectories into OSWorld-Persona, a benchmark with persona-conditioned intervention labels. On OSWorld-Persona, deep personalization improves macro F1 across three model backbones from 0.12-0.19 under direct prompting to 0.35-0.48 after adaptation, a 2.4-3.0x relative gain. In a week-long user study, we observe that Coco improves its macro-averaged F1 score from 0.199 to 0.515. These results suggest that on-device deep personalization can make proactive agents more timely and increasingly aligned with each user's everyday work.
evidence_items.title: Deep Personalization: Continuous Context Observation for Local Proactive Agents

evidence_items.summary: System-1 Decision Models directly make structured probabilistic decisions over query-specified options given a state in a single forward pass, without autoregressively generating reasoning trajectories or textual responses. Recent evaluations cover diverse tasks but often rely on existing benchmarks, where prior exposure to test material can obscure generalization. Moreover, real-world decision making often involves long contexts, large option spaces, and complex logical dependencies, challenges that existing benchmarks do not adequately capture together. Thus, we introduce MMDM (Massive Multitask Decision Making), a benchmark of 5,448 high-quality questions across 16 task categories, combining newly constructed tasks with source-grounded recompositions and rewrites for single-select, multi-select, and soft-label decision making in fresh contexts. It covers realistic scenarios such as agent state tracking, tool and skill selection, preference judgments, and rubric scoring, with option spaces ranging from 2 to 1,024 and inputs extending to 64,817 tokens. With MMDM, we conduct a comprehensive quantitative evaluation of 28 decision models, showing that many perform well on common knowledge yet struggle with interdependent options, constrained decisions, and multi-select tasks. For example, Perplexity Decider-V1.2 reaches 78.75% Hard Single-select Accuracy on world knowledge, but only 53.95% on option logic and 47.95% on constraint planning, while the best Hard Multi-select Accuracy across all models is 36.81%. These results highlight joint reasoning, constraint-aware selection, and complete multi-select recovery as key priorities for decision model development, with MMDM providing a testbed for measuring this progress.
evidence_items.title: MMDM: Measuring Massive Multitask Decision Making

evidence_items.summary: Under a fixed frame budget, video understanding with vision-language models (VLMs) depends on whether the sampled frames provide sufficient evidence for the question. Sufficient frame evidence supports direct answering, whereas less informative observations may benefit from reasoning that connects the available cues. We introduce EVAThink, which enhances video understanding through evidence sufficiency-guided training for adaptive thinking. First, Recoverable Evidence Gap Mining constructs evidence-dense and evidence-sparse video views that share the same question and answer under an identical frame budget. It retains pairs where sparse views yield lower direct-answer accuracy than dense views but benefit from explicit reasoning, providing supervision for response-mode selection. Second, Evidence-Guided Two-Stage Reinforcement Learning uses stage-specific rewards to guide training with evidence-based mode preferences and then refine response efficiency, while first-token advantage regularization mitigates mode collapse. Trained on only 6.7K curated samples, EVAThink consistently improves upon the base model across video understanding benchmarks under both 32- and 64-frame budgets, while outperforming strong baselines on average. The code, model, and datasets are available at https://github.com/ChangtiWu/EVAThink{EVAThink}.
evidence_items.title: EVAThink: Evidence Sufficiency-Guided Training for Adaptive Thinking in Video Understanding

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used in intelligent teaching and cognitive-level classification. However, mainstream Transformer architectures incur redundant attention computation, and a single feed-forward network struggles to perform the fine-grained routing of features for Bloom’s cognitive features. This study proposes BACE, an educational LLM for cognitive-level text classification based on an asymmetric hybrid architecture guided by Bloom’s taxonomy. Built on the pretrained ChatGLM3-6B, BACE replaces the MLP in the first 4 layers with a shallow Top-2 sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) routing module to achieve token-level dispatching of cognitive features while retaining the self-attention mechanism. The middle 20 layers retain the native self-attention and MLP structures to maintain semantic transition. In the last 4 layers, attention is replaced with a deep, selective state-space modeling strategy, combined with chain-of-thought fine-tuning based on Bloom’s taxonomy, to integrate the global instructional context. Experiments on a public computer science course question dataset across multiple random seeds show that BACE achieves an average accuracy of 73.56% and a weighted F1 score of 0.6915, improving on ChatGLM3-6B (65.78%/0.6011) by 7.78 percentage points and 0.0904, respectively. Although its accuracy and weighted F1 are slightly lower than those of Qwen1.5-7B, BACE attains a BLEU-4 of 0.3426 and a ROUGE-L of 0.4601 on the generated chain-of-thought reasoning, both outperforming open-source models including Qwen1.5-7B, Mistral-7B, and Llama-3-8B. Through its asymmetric hybrid architecture, the model enables the classification of Bloom’s cognitive levels and provides a scalable technical pathway for question-answering-based cognitive-level assessment in intelligent education scenarios.
evidence_items.title: BACE: Bloom’s Asymmetric Hybrid Cognitive-Level Classification Educational Large Language Model

evidence_items.summary: Graphene nanopores can, in principle, combine high water permeability with strong salt rejection, but finding pore geometries that do both usually requires many molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. We describe a design framework in which a large language model (LLM) grows a nanopore atom by atom, using pretrained predictors of water flux and ion rejection to judge each candidate. Two recent models, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, were tested with the same prompt and the same design protocol (30 steps, up to 30 trials per step, at most three atoms removed per trial, and a 90% ion-rejection floor). We wanted to know how much of an agent’s performance comes from the model and how much from the surrounding scaffold, so each model was run twice: once as a tool-using agent with access to the predictors, and once in conversation only, where it chose atoms and estimated performance without any feedback. Three scaffold-only baselines that contain no language model were run for comparison. With tools, both models stayed above the rejection floor at every step. Claude Opus 5.5 produced a single, island-free pore with a predicted flux of 122.3 ns−1 at 93.2% rejection, and GPT-6.1 Sol reached 131.7 ns−1 at 90.2%. Without tools the two models erred in opposite directions. Claude Opus 5.5 overestimated rejection and removed too many atoms, ending at 64.3% rejection, whereas GPT-6.1 Sol was overly cautious and recovered only 30% of the flux reached by its scaffold. A greedy search restricted by simple manufacturability rules matched or exceeded both agents in flux. Compared with the MD dataset and the deep reinforcement learning (DRL) designs of earlier work, the agents placed a larger share of their high-rejection pores above 120 ns−1. Taken together, the results indicate that predictor feedback, rather than the language model on its own, is what keeps LLM-guided pore design on target, and the six-condition protocol gives a simple way to make that attribution for other models.

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in medical imaging, with research spanning task-specific classification, detection, and segmentation, representation learning, image reconstruction, generative models, foundation models, and vision–language models (VLMs). This review synthesizes 74 core publications and organizes them into four groups: task-specific image analysis; representation learning and image reconstruction; generative and generalist models; and robustness, generalizability, and clinical evaluation. Across these research directions, reported performance is shaped by data sources, patient-level separation, acquisition conditions, label quality, model adaptation, and validation design. Generative and multimodal systems also raise questions about factual consistency and clinical use. Among the 45 primary empirical studies in the selected core set, multicentre evaluation and temporal/prospective evaluation were each assigned as the primary evaluation profile to one study. No prospective interventional or randomized clinical evaluation was identified within this core set. The review summarizes methodological developments and evaluation challenges and discusses priorities for reliable medical imaging AI, including external validation and evaluation in intended clinical settings.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Medical Imaging: From Task-Specific Models to Clinical Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Drug development remains a costly and time-consuming process since identifying therapeutic targets that are both biologically relevant and clinically effective remains challenging. New technologies including bulk RNA sequencing, single-cell RNA sequencing, CRISPR screens and AI are enabling new target discovery opportunities, but there are still a number of challenges in bringing the heterogeneous data sets together. This paper describes how AI-assisted integration of these three technologies can improve drug development. This paper explains in detail how Bulk RNA sequencing can detect differentially expressed genes, how Single-cell RNA sequencing can uncover cell-specific expression patterns, how CRISPR screening can identify dependencies of genes in disease-related phenotypes, and how AI models can recognize complex molecular patterns and prioritize targets for therapeutic intervention using these complementary datasets. With AI support and current technologies, researchers could decrease false-positive target identification and enhance drug sensitivity forecasting. This paper suggest a way to improve the precision-drug-discovery strategies. But there are still issues with data heterogeneity and with model interpretability. To address the remaining challenges, interpretable AI models that combine multi-omics, functional genomic, and patient-derived data should be developed in the future.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence Assistance with CRISPR to Optimize Drug Development

evidence_items.summary: Tennis players' technical movements, movements, spatial behavior, and other aspects during matches can already be well analyzed by artificial intelligence, but the data and game predictions obtained from these analyses still need to be integrate. This is the research direction of this narrative review. This review summarizes the relevant data sources, calculation methods, technical features, performance indicators, and prediction methods. Based on technical action information, a comprehensive discussion was conducted around the main line of "from analyzing performance indicators to final prediction", and the relationship between research at different levels was elaborated. At the same time, this review also indicates that videos, Hawk-Eye technology, and wearable devices during matches can provide sufficient information on players' movement and spatial use; These data captured through external devices and analyzed by artificial intelligence need to be combined with the competition context in order to be used as supplementary data for in-game prediction. On this basis, this review proposes research directions for connecting action analysis with whole game prediction, including unified indicators and label definitions, prediction based on standard time series, and comparison using time series validation, probability calibration, and traditional benchmark models. This comprehensive technology provides a clear analytical approach that not only helps to understand the contribution of artificial intelligence in tennis analysis, but also provides new ideas for future game predictions.

evidence_items.summary: Traffic and industrial emissions sustain background PM 2.5 pollution in Southeast Asia. Seasonal peatland and agricultural fires produce transboundary haze. Monsoon winds carry that pollution between countries. Rainfall removes particles from the atmosphere. Chemical reactions during transport can also form secondary aerosols before polluted air reaches downwind cities. This review examines how atmospheric processes affect model evaluation and assesses the reported accuracy. Data-driven algorithms track normal concentration changes, but their accuracy varies between studies and tests. Differences in predictors, validation setups and satellite data availability limit comparisons between studies. Some models show larger errors during extreme PM 2.5 events, at unseen stations or across different monsoon seasons. Feature attribution scores show how algorithms work internally, but they do not show actual physical emission sources. Evaluations should report separate scores for severe haze days, test geographically withheld stations and assess physical consistency against chemical transport models. Standardized data for Mainland and Maritime Southeast Asia can help assess whether new algorithms support public health warnings.

evidence_items.summary: This work proposes WaveGen, a fully end-to-end diffusion-based text-to-waveform framework based on Spectral Forcing, which jointly learns an internal spectral trajectory and the target waveform trajectory within a single model, enabling direct end-to-end text-to-waveform generation. Unlike recent TTS pipelines, WaveGen does not rely on separately trained or externally decoded intermediate representations, such as neural audio codecs, Mel-spectrogram vocoders, or VAE-based latent models. In addition, WaveGen performs internal text-speech alignment within a single model, eliminating the need for external alignment modules such as duration predictors. To preserve a truly end-to-end formulation, our framework further avoids dependence on self-supervised representations, such as BERT-based text embeddings and Wav2Vec 2.0-based semantic representations, as well as semantic distillation methods for training optimization. To achieve this, we carefully design Spectral Forcing, a model architecture with disentangled diffusion heads, and a training objective based on a multi-scale spectral v-loss. We further validate the scalability of end-to-end TTS models by scaling the model size from 0.1B to 0.6B parameters. Using a single architecture, open-source data, and one-stage training, without external modules such as duration predictor or REPA, WaveGen demonstrates fully end-to-end waveform generation achieving state-of-the-art performance on the Emilia training dataset. In particular, WaveGen achieves a WER of 1.47 and a SIM of 0.75 on the Seed-en benchmark. Source code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/sh-lee-prml/WaveGen
evidence_items.title: WaveGen: Truly End-to-End Waveform Generation via Internal Spectral Trajectory Learning

F254  QUANTUM SENSOR CROSS-SITE CALIBRATION TRANSFER AT THE LIMIT — Core: ODMR microwave-frequency reference transfer; photodetector spectral response mismatch. Witness: cross-site bias [nT]. Comparator: independent site-specific NIST-traceable calibration and a frozen classical sensor transfer. Rival: true magnetic field shift. Stop: untraceable reference ancestry or unsafe calibration release under failed commutability. F255  NANOROBOTIC MISSION RELIABILITY STATISTICS AT THE LIMIT — Core: early mission failure censoring; recovery-conditional survival bias. Witness: mission completion probability [dimensionless]. Comparator: fixed-limit statistical process control with transparent unselected failure registry. Rival: improved mission reliability. Stop: a hazardous failure has no traceable state or is incorrectly classified as safe.   RESEARCH UNIT II  /  RECONSTRUCTION, RECOVERY AND SUCCESSION F256  MICROSCALE EXPERIMENT REPEAT-MEASUREMENT BIAS AT THE LIMIT — Core: measurement sequence effect; sensor warm-up effect. Witness: paired measurement bias [native units]. Comparator: randomized blinded single-site repeatability with external second-operator reference. Rival: true specimen ageing. Stop: unidentified systematic error exceeds the preregistered accuracy margin. F257  QUANTUM BIOSENSING RIVAL-MODEL VALIDATION AT THE LIMIT — Core: spin-state dependent fluorescence; surface adsorption optical rival. Witness: held-out calibrated log score [nats per case]. Comparator: optimized classical biosensing model with matched photons and full nuisance adjustment. Rival: laser-intensity noise. Stop: an unmodeled biological or optical burden is misclassified as validated quantum gain. F258  NANOROBOTIC POST-FAILURE SAFE RECOVERY AT THE LIMIT — Core: nonresponsive actuator shutdown; physical isolation valve reliability. Witness: safe recovery success probability [dimensionless]. Comparator: manual emergency shutoff with passive containment and supervised retrieval. Rival: software status bit says stopped. Stop: continued actuation after a veto or irreversible sample identity loss. F259  MICROFLUIDIC RESEARCH PLATFORM FAULT INJECTION AT THE LIMIT — Core: valve mechanically stuck open; pressure-sensor failure. Witness: hidden-fault detection recall [dimensionless]. Comparator: conventional alarm thresholds with a calibrated operator-supervised closed-chip test. Rival: software valve-position indication. Stop: uncontained biological sample or failure to close pressure mass and valve-state evidence. F260  QUANTUM SENSOR COVARIANT ERROR RECONSTRUCTION AT THE LIMIT — Core: common calibration-reference drift; latent thermal common cause. Witness: held-out joint interval coverage [dimensionless]. Comparator: full-covariance generalized least squares against diagonal-only error propagation. Rival: true co-varying magnetic signal. Stop: a physically impossible covariance or unreported common-mode uncertainty enters a release decision. Physical Scope & Scientific Boundaries Restricted to material-identified, nonclinical, closed-chip bench work, with independent observation, prespecified resource-matched controls, complete specimen denominators, concealed perturbations and hard physical stops. Proposed equations and original research designs are not measurements. The mother-record DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23318840 supplies editorial lineage; independently verified peer-reviewed article links should be checked for direct relevance before any experimental claim. Automated twelve-word overlap and exact-paragraph checks quantify repeated phrasing but cannot establish scientific independence. evidence_items.summary: Reliable dermatology AI requires access to verifiable evidence distributed across heterogeneous textual and visual sources. However, conventional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) typically relies on one-shot retrieval from flat corpora, limiting its ability to adapt retrieval granularity, explore multi-hop relations, and integrate multimodal clinical evidence. We introduce SkinMind, a multimodal agentic RAG framework that equips policy models with human-inspired graph probing for autonomous evidence seeking. SkinMind organizes retrieval as an iterative interaction between an orchestrator and a graph environment. Through eight hierarchical graph-probing tools, the orchestrator progressively identifies relevant entities, inspects node-level information, traverses relations and paths, and retrieves source-text and visual evidence. This progressive-disclosure design allows the model to adaptively determine the retrieval modality, exploration direction, and evidence granularity while constructing a query-specific evidence subgraph. To support autonomous graph probing, we construct SkinMind-KG from a 62M-token corpus of dermatology guidelines and textbooks and 423K images, guided by a dermatologist-informed schema and a conflict-resolution mechanism. The resulting graph contains over 1.0M nodes and 2.0M edges, unifying textual, relational, and visual evidence for retrieval. Across six dermatology VQA benchmarks and two policy-model settings, SkinMind improves the average score over direct answering by 8.70 and 8.89 points with GPT-5.4-mini and Gemini-2.5-Flash, respectively, while consistently outperforming competing RAG methods. Together, SkinMind and SkinMind-KG provide an effective foundation for evidence-grounded multimodal reasoning in dermatology.
evidence_items.title: SkinMind: Equipping Agentic RAG with Human-Inspired Graph Probing for Reliable Dermatology AI

evidence_items.summary: Discrete autoregressive modeling, notably through next-token prediction, has become a cornerstone of modern language models. Extending this paradigm to vision allows visual and language models to converge on a unified framework, thereby fostering shared methodology and infrastructure. This work investigates a central question: how far can a finite discrete vocabulary go in representing the richness of the visual world? We present dNaViT, a Discrete Native-resolution Vision Transformer that produces discrete visual primitives analogous to language tokens. Built upon a frozen pretrained encoder, dNaViT applies lightweight residual modulation with a dual-branch objective to inject reconstruction-aware cues into semantic features. By leveraging grouped product quantization, it scales discrete capacity without inflating spatial sequence lengths, while a balanced training recipe maintains both semantic and pixel-level information. Consequently, dNaViT functions as a versatile discrete visual tokenizer, enabling unified encoding across downstream tasks alongside high-fidelity image decoding. Extensive evaluations show that dNaViT matches or exceeds task-specific baselines across 12 visual understanding benchmarks, 4 generation benchmarks, and an image editing benchmark. These findings demonstrate that a compact discrete vocabulary can serve as a universal visual currency and unlock the full potential of fully unified, native multimodal methodology.
evidence_items.title: dNaViT: Discrete Codes are General-Purpose Visual Representations

evidence_items.summary: We introduce FraudBench, an evaluation of large language models' (LLMs) propensities to recommend, assist, or directly take actions that would constitute fraud under U.S. law. Our evaluation contains a novel dataset of 159 scenarios based on real-world U.S. court cases and validated by legal experts. We present each scenario to LLMs via three tasks at varying levels of autonomy: advising users, drafting messages for users to send, and acting directly on behalf of users (477 tasks total). In each scenario, FraudBench re-enacts the facts of a court case to give LLMs an opportunity, but no explicit instruction, to either misrepresent or conceal a material fact in a high-stakes commercial setting--e.g., whether to describe company-funded product testing as "independent" to customers (misrepresentation) or whether to hide unfavorable regulatory investigations from clients (concealment). We evaluate 20 LLMs across 25 experimental conditions (totaling >300,000 generations) and include a preregistered human baseline (n_{annotations} = 2{,}957, n_{humans} = 996). We score a response as fraudulent when it engages in, assists with, or recommends misrepresentation or concealment. Key findings include: (1) across LLMs, fraud rates ranged from near 0% to over 40%; (2) LLM fraud rates increased with autonomy, with overall rates of 3.0% when advising, 14.7% when drafting, and 21.4% when acting directly, without applying pressure; (3) LLMs sometimes engaged in fraud despite recognizing legal risks; (4) LLMs more often engaged in fraud by concealment than by misrepresentation; and (5) prompt-based interventions substantially affected fraud rates, with a prompt to obey the law reducing fraud rates, while prompts to maximize profits and act agentically increased fraud rates.
evidence_items.title: FraudBench: A Legal Evaluation of AI Deception

evidence_items.summary: Despite impressive progress, existing feed-forward large 3D reconstruction models produce a single, irrevocable prediction. When these models fail, there is no mechanism to correct their mistakes. To address this limitation, we introduce Click3R, a framework for interactive geometric correction of feed-forward models using sparse human correspondence clicks. Given an image pair and a small set of cross-view point correspondences provided by a user, Click3R injects geometric constraints into the 3D reconstruction networks through a lightweight point correspondence adapter, enabling the model to resolve ambiguities in challenging scenarios such as repetitive textures, symmetric structures, large viewpoint changes, or textureless regions. To evaluate interactive reconstruction, we curate a challenging benchmark specifically designed to expose failure modes of existing feed-forward 3D reconstruction methods. Experiments show that Click3R reduces reconstruction error with as few as a single correspondence click, improving performance on both standard and our curated benchmarks. Our results highlight that sparse human interaction provides an effective and practical mechanism for correcting geometric reconstruction errors.
evidence_items.title: Click3R: Interactive Stereo 3D Reconstruction with Sparse Correspondence Clicks

evidence_items.summary: Self-supervised learning in Vision Transformer models, such as DINO, enables robust visual perception without requiring labeled data by leveraging large-scale image datasets. However, these models lack a focusing mechanism during training, resulting in perceptual representations that are often ambiguous or overly similar. In this work, we introduce two visual focusing loss functions designed to establish correspondence between the model's attention and specific regions within images. Specifically, we leverage the multi-head attention mechanism within the model to selectively steer the model's focus, leading to the emergence of spatial attention head specialization, characterized by diverse and spatially focused perceptual capabilities without requiring annotations. Through both qualitative and quantitative evaluations, we demonstrate that our method substantially increases the spatial selectivity and diversity of attention heads, improving both interpretability and performance on dense prediction tasks such as zero-shot image segmentation.
evidence_items.title: Training Vision Transformers to Focus: Emergence of Spatial Attention Head Specialization

evidence_items.summary: Visual generative models increasingly blur the line between synthesizing observations and simulating environments. Yet visual plausibility alone does not constitute successful world modeling: compelling outputs may lack persistent state, physical dynamics, or causally consistent responses to interactions. We define a generative world model as a predictive dynamical system that maintains a persistent, history-conditioned representation of an environment, updates that representation in response to actions or interventions, and generates temporally coherent trajectories that reflect outcomes under observed and counterfactual interventions. From this definition, we derive an intelligence-oriented framework spanning perceptual grounding, persistent state modeling, controllable transformation, dynamics-aware prediction, and closed-loop interaction. We present WorldFoundry, open-source infrastructure for reproducible inference and evaluation across video, 3D and 4D, embodied action, and interactive world systems. WorldFoundry unifies model and benchmark discovery, runtime and asset preparation, execution orchestration, artifact management, and interactive visualization, while modality-specific adapters preserve native inputs, execution semantics, output representations, and evaluation protocols. Explicit manifests, durable artifact contracts, and evidence-aware scorecards separate execution readiness from evaluative claims, making each claim traceable to its supporting artifacts. The catalog contains 270 model entries, 74 benchmarks, and 62 registered metric entries, with readiness and execution evidence recorded separately. WorldFoundry enables reproducible comparison of persistent, controllable dynamics across heterogeneous systems, advancing the field from perceptual synthesis toward measurable world intelligence.
evidence_items.title: WorldFoundry: Towards Unified Infrastructure for World Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: Real-time 3D human mesh recovery from a single image on mobile devices is a challenging problem with many applications, including robotics, biomechanics, AR/VR, and exergames. Current state-of-the-art models are either too slow to run efficiently on mobile devices or sacrifice accuracy for speed. We present InstantHMR, a family of open-source single-image regressors suited for mobile inference, based on the Momentum Human Rig (MHR) parametric model and trained exclusively on publicly available annotations from the SAM 3D Body dataset. Our approach achieves remarkable performance on a Samsung Galaxy S23 NPU, recovering a 6,890-vertex body mesh in 5.5 ms per person, and 0.98 ms on an NVIDIA RTX 4070 GPU. This speed surpasses all existing methods we evaluated. On mobile, it is 12x faster than the single mobile-compatible method that slightly outperforms ours in accuracy, while achieving competitive accuracy with 40.0 mm PA-MPJPE on 3DPW, 48.8 mm on EMDB and 41.7 mm on RICH. To ensure fair comparisons, we re-evaluate 11 state-of-the-art methods under a unified protocol aligned with the closest MHR-based competitors, including Meta's official MHR-to-SMPL conversion, and report their reproduction results. Additionally, we measure latency across eight different targets, ranging from desktop TensorRT to two phone NPUs. Code and models are available at https://github.com/Naturalpad-studio/InstantHMR.
evidence_items.title: InstantHMR : Real-Time Human Mesh Recovery on Your Phone

evidence_items.summary: LLM agents increasingly drive systems research and rely on simulators to evaluate candidate designs at scale. Simulators are imperfect by design: their modeling limitations can distort predictions yet leave the recommended design correct, or change which design should be selected. We introduce Siris to test whether LLMs can tell these cases apart, judging from their systems understanding when a limitation invalidates the simulator's recommendation. By perturbing a simulator, Siris constructs workload pairs with the same candidates, limitation, and simulator recommendation. The perturbation changes predictions on both workloads, yet a reference simulator supports the recommendation on only one. Evaluating thirteen frontier LLMs on LLM serving design problems, we find that identifying a limitation does not ensure a correct choice, and even the strongest models sometimes abandon valid recommendations. Self-correction through a review turn helps these models restore valid choices but introduces new errors in several others. These findings motivate evaluating systems understanding through design decisions under imperfect simulators.
evidence_items.title: SIRIS: Can LLMs Tell When Simulation Errors Matter in AI-Driven Systems Research

evidence_items.summary: Reproducing machine learning experiments requires reconstructing procedures from information scattered across papers, released code, and supporting artifacts. For coding agents, reproduction success can therefore depend on their ability to fill in missing details, rather than on the released artifacts alone. We ask whether preserving recovered procedures and decisions improves subsequent independent reproduction. We define a standardized artifact design comprising a refined codebase, environment setup, experiment launchers, and a reproduction guide, and introduce ReproBridge, an agent workflow for constructing these refined reproducible artifacts. ReproBridge-Bench provides 1,029 tasks from 387 experiments across 36 papers, anchored by five human-verified reference scores per task. Agents attempt tasks in fresh sessions with raw code or refined artifacts; a separate Auditor checks execution evidence. Across four evaluated models, refined artifacts raise mean reproduction success from 76.4% to 92.6% and reduce downstream API spending by 19.7% on average. The cross-model success-rate spread narrows from 21.6 to 3.9 percentage points, with all four models achieving mean success rates above 90%. Removing any component reduces success in the ablation study, with the largest losses from code and environment removal. These results suggest that preserving execution knowledge helps even models with lower raw-code success reproduce experiments more reliably and at lower API cost.
evidence_items.title: ReproBridge: Building Reproducibility into ML Research Artifacts

evidence_items.summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) enables multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to scale capacity efficiently, but expert parameters dominate memory even though only a few experts are activated per token: they account for over 90% of model size in modern MoE-MLLMs (e.g., 54 GB out of about 58 GB in BF16 for InternVL3.5-30B-A3B and Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B). Expert pruning has emerged as an effective compression strategy, but existing methods aggregate importance uniformly across tokens, ignoring that the same expert may serve different roles for vision versus language processing. To address this, we propose MAEP (Modality-Aware Expert Pruning), a training-free framework that decomposes expert importance by modality in a single forward pass. MAEP introduces (1) Delta-H Output (ΔH), a redistribution-aware metric measuring the MoE output change when an expert is removed, and (2) low-attention vision tokens as a vision-side pruning signal that is dataset-stable: its expert-importance ranking remains stable across different datasets. Text-side importance serves as a preservation signal while vision-side importance serves as a pruning signal, and experts are ranked globally across layers. Experiments on three MoE-based MLLMs across multimodal and text benchmarks show that MAEP outperforms modality-agnostic baselines on the majority of multimodal benchmarks while remaining competitive on text-only tasks, reducing the BF16 expert weight footprint by about 27 GB (about 47% of total memory) so that the full weight footprint of an approximately 58 GB model fits within a single 40 GB GPU. Code is available at https://github.com/nota-github/MAEP.
evidence_items.title: Modality-Aware Expert Pruning for MoE-Based Multimodal Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: This paper studies retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which leverages external knowledge to improve the performance of language models. Despite the remarkable progress, current RAG approaches are still far from satisfactory due to inadequate retrieval and potential hallucinations. Towards this end, we propose a novel approach named Task Refinement with Individual Optimization (TRIO) for RAG. The core idea of our TRIO is to equip three well-designed agents with an iterative refinement paradigm by aligning their individual optimization objectives. Specifically, we first expand ambiguous queries with a query extension agent and quantify the reward based on the improved answer quality, which can be utilized to refine our agent for higher expansion efficiency. To enhance the retrieval quality, we include a unanimity voting to annotate the expanded query as insufficient or sufficient, and their generative outcomes are utilized as ground truth to optimize the judge agent. To further improve evidence utilization and answer accuracy, an answer agent is optimized with dynamic matching-based rewards with curriculum learning for final outputs. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmark datasets validate the effectiveness of the proposed TRIO in comparison with state-of-the-art approaches. Our code is available at https://github.com/yingtaoren/TRIO.
evidence_items.title: TRIO: Task Refinement with Individual Optimization for Retrieval-Augmented Generation

evidence_items.summary: Decision models such as Jev have emerged as a highly promising paradigm for LLM agent systems, providing lightweight and reliable categorical reasoning for rapid System One execution. However, existing generation-oriented inference engines fail to support these workloads effectively, suffering from severe prefix recomputation overheads or distorted output probabilities. To address this challenge, we propose Flide, an efficient and exact inference engine that decouples the logical tree structure of a decision request from its physical execution within a single flattened token stream. Through ForkAttention, Flide navigates request dependencies using GPU-resident indices across both standard attention and recurrent Gated DeltaNet layers, guaranteeing in exact arithmetic that every query branch evaluates identically to an isolated forward pass. By expressing branch topologies directly in GPU-resident metadata, Flide accommodates diverse request mixtures with a compact set of pre-recorded execution graphs while enabling expanding agent histories to resume from checkpoints saved in earlier passes. Extensive evaluations on public hybrid and decision models demonstrate that Flide answers queries up to 9.5 times faster than vLLM and SGLang while staying closest to a float32 reference in total variation distance. By unifying physical execution throughput with mathematical exactness, Flide establishes a principled foundation for scalable, latency-critical decision intelligence in agent systems.
evidence_items.title: Flide: Accelerating Decision Inference with Exact State Forking

The package contains aggregate endpoint and statistical outputs, model-configuration and execution metadata, sanitized prompt/schema/ontology artifacts and hashes, scoring and statistical code, figure-source data, reproducible figure renderings, Supplementary Materials, corrected-cohort provenance documentation, and audit records. All 2,430 LLM outputs retained in the final analysis originated from the original multi-model execution period; no API calls were repeated for the corrected N=486 analysis. evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background The assessment of the risk of bias (RoB) of each study is a necessary but labor-intensive step in conducting a systematic review (SR). There is a potential for AI to reduce the time and effort needed for RoB assessment and improve consistency between reviewers, but little is known about the accuracy of AI-based RoB assessments. Objective In this study, we aim to evaluate the performance of a large language model (LLM) when given the questions from the RoB tool and the relevant passages from the full-text papers in assessing RoB in observational studies of environmental exposures and health outcomes. Methods We evaluated the performance of GPT-5-mini on 128 observational studies from a SR of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances and health outcomes conducted by the National Academies of Sciences. The navigation guide (NavGuide), a domain-based RoB tool designed for environmental studies, was used. For each paper-domain pair, the LLM was provided with the questions and guidance from the NavGuide and the human-identified text passages addressing that domain. The LLM returned a structured RoB rating, which was compared to the human-adjudicated ratings to quantify agreement and identify patterns of discrepancy. Results GPT-5-mini RoB assessments for exact matches (64.5%; κ=0.199, Gwet AC2=0.882, F 1 score=0.311) remained lower than the concordance between humans and the reference standard (87.5%-91.4%). Performance improved substantially for partial matches, reflecting agreement in direction but not necessarily in magnitude (eg, “low” and “probably low”), with percent concordance of 91.9% (κ=0.241, Gwet AC2=0.910, F 1 score=0.614; for humans, 97.9%-98.6% concordance). Performance varied across the NavGuide domains, with the worst performance in domain 1 (selection bias) and the best in domain 4 (outcome assessment). The models tended to be more stringent than humans, often assigning higher RoB ratings (eg, “probably low” when humans assigned “low”).
evidence_items.title: Large Language Model Risk of Bias Assessment for Studies in Environmental Health: Proof-of-Concept Study

evidence_items.summary: Introduction Watershed environmental governance increasingly combines dense sensing infrastructure with institutions whose attention, authority, and coordination capacity remain limited. We develop the cognitive orchestration layer as a theory-building concept for examining how large language model (LLM)-based agents may connect sensing, assessment, decision advice, institutional response, and feedback without displacing domain models or public authority. Methods The Agentic Framework for Watershed Governance (AFWG) specifies three enabling pathways, three institutional interfaces, and four propositions. A purposively selected set of eight publicly documented cases is used to illustrate functional configurations, source limitations, and research gaps; it is not a systematic review or empirical evaluation. Results The cases document sensing, assessment, and decision-support functions, but do not establish improved decision quality, sustained institutional use, environmental outcomes, or agent-executed response closure. MAESTRO is retained as an adjacent-domain design illustration, not an existence proof of full-loop closure: human authorization remains necessary, and its reported performance has not been independently replicated. Discussion Transfer to watershed governance is plausible only where domain models remain authoritative, outputs carry provenance and uncertainty, named officials retain authority to authorize consequential actions, and institutional audit and failure handling are built into deployment. AFWG therefore offers a bounded conceptual framework and a falsifiable research agenda, rather than a claim that agents have already closed the watershed response loop.
evidence_items.title: Large language model agents in watershed environmental response: a hypothesis-and-theory framework for the cognitive orchestration layer

evidence_items.summary: Claude Lévi-Strauss’s structuralism offers a useful perspective on large language models (LLMs) through its emphasis on relationships within systems of meaning. This paper recalls relational meaning, oppositions and mediation, transformations, and bricolage, illustrating these ideas through Lévi-Strauss’s analysis of myth and an everyday example of gift-giving. It then examines their connections with contextual representations and generative processes in LLMs. These connections support a productive comparison, although similarities do not establish that language models implement or validate structuralist theory. Practical implications include assessing whether models preserve relevant relationships across reformulations, examining the cultural categories expressed in their responses, and distinguishing coherent explanations from empirically justified claims. Structuralism can inform the interpretation and evaluation of LLM behaviour, while LLMs offer opportunities to investigate how relationships are learned, represented and transformed. The comparison therefore provides a basis for exploring meaning and creativity, with attention to the differences between linguistic competence, cultural understanding and knowledge of the world.
evidence_items.title: Meaning through Relations: Lévi-Strauss and Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Accurate diameter-at-breast-height (DBH) measurement is essential for forest inventory and ecological monitoring. This work evaluates two AI-assisted smartphone frameworks: a text-prompt Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM3) that segments trunks from red-green-blue (RGB) images, and a depth-guided MobileSAM model that uses depth cues to generate geometry-based prompts. The resulting masks are integrated into a geometric pipeline for DBH estimation. The proposed frameworks combine AI-based trunk segmentation with geometry-guided DBH measurement to improve the accuracy, interpretability, and practical efficiency of smartphone-based DBH estimation, with the depth-guided MobileSAM framework enabling near real-time use and the SAM3 for its robustness and accuracy despite of the high computational power requirement.&#xD;Both methods were tested on 202 planted and 285 natural trees. In planted forests, both achieved high accuracy with no failures (root mean square error, RMSE: 1.2 cm for SAM3, 1.1 cm for MobileSAM). In natural forests, SAM3 remained robust (1.7 cm RMSE), while MobileSAM failed in four cases and showed lower accuracy (2.4 cm RMSE excluding failures).&#xD;MobileSAM runs in ~0.89 s per image on a smartphone, enabling near real-time use. SAM3 is much slower on CPU (~160 s on 12th Gen Intel(R) Core(TM) i7-1260P) but can be accelerated on GPUs (0.13 s on A100, 3.71 s on T4). Overall, MobileSAM is more practical for on-device deployment, while SAM3 offers greater robustness in complex environments but requires high-performance hardware.
evidence_items.title: Artificial intelligence-assisted tree diameter-at-breast-height measurement

evidence_items.summary: Higher levels of anxiety about artificial intelligence (AI) among older and less-educated adults have now been documented in large population-based samples from high-income countries. Much less is known about how these differences arise, whether age and education interact, and whether occupational position helps understand them, particularly in middle-income economies. It evaluates the measurement structure of the scale, tests flexible functional forms and age–education interactions, and decomposes both gradients by occupational skill level, task class, and routine-task intensity. AI anxiety increases approximately linearly with age, whereas its association with education is strongly negative and nonlinear, with the largest gap between the lowest and highest education categories. Age and education largely show additive associations with AI anxiety. The age gradient is weaker among university graduates, although evidence for an interaction is limited for the total score and more evident for several subdimensions. Among the 409 employed respondents, occupational skill level and task class substantially reduce the education gradient but leave the age gradient unchanged: labor-market position helps explain educational but not age differences. Routine-task intensity contributes little beyond broad occupational categories, while professionals and managers report relatively high anxiety conditional on education and task class. Because the cross-sectional design precludes causal and age-period-cohort interpretations, the estimates are conditional associations. Even so, the results show that AI anxiety is not randomly distributed: it is systematically structured by human capital, age, and occupational position in a large middle-income economy.
evidence_items.title: Age, Education, and Occupational Gradients in Artificial Intelligence Anxiety

evidence_items.summary: The widespread integration of artificial intelligence systems into everyday and professional practices challenges classical philosophical conceptions of agency, autonomy, and responsibility. Under conditions of algorithmic mediation, human action is increasingly shaped within hybrid sociotechnical systems in which cognitive, epistemic, and normative functions are distributed between humans and AI. This situation calls for a reexamination of which properties of agency remain distinctively human and how they manifest within this new configuration of human–AI interaction. The aim of this article is to provide a philosophical analysis of the specific properties of human agency in hybrid human–artificial intelligence systems and to identify how intentionality and control are transformed under algorithmic mediation. The article demonstrates that human agency in AI-mediated sociotechnical systems is characterized by weakened epistemic autonomy, contextually distributed control, and a hybrid form of intentionality that incorporates algorithmically generated elements. The article identifies several distinctive features, including vulnerability to algorithmic framing and cognitive codependence on AI systems, that distinguish hybrid agency from classical instrumental models of human action. The article concludes that, despite these transformations, humans retain a unique role in normative reflection and meaning-making. This role enables them to critically evaluate and reconfigure the architectures that structure interaction with AI. The article is intended for philosophers, media scholars, digital technology researchers, specialists in AI ethics, and others engaged in analyzing sociotechnical systems and questions of responsibility in algorithmically mediated social realities.
evidence_items.title: Human Agency under Conditions of Algorithmic Mediation by Artificial Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: The penetration of artificial intelligence (AI) into rural industries is reshaping the underlying logic of integration among the primary, secondary and tertiary sectors in rural areas. Based on a systematic review of the relevant literature, this paper develops a four-dimensional analytical framework—technological penetration, actor empowerment, network restructuring and value co-creation—to explain the micro-level mechanisms through which AI drives rural industrial integration. The analysis shows that AI reduces information asymmetry by embedding data as a production factor, alters the resource endowments and bargaining power of diverse business actors through tool-based empowerment and knowledge diffusion, reshapes the distribution of benefits by restructuring collaborative networks, and ultimately manifests itself in industrial chain extension, value chain upgrading and the sharing of value-added gains. Accordingly, drawing on resource endowments, industrial foundations and locational conditions, villages are classified into three types—peri-urban technology-integrated villages, specialty agriculture–empowered villages and eco-cultural tourism innovation villages—for which differentiated integration pathways are identified. A three-tier dynamic evaluation indicator system covering foundational support, integrative application, and impacts and benefits is then constructed. The paper argues that the extent to which smallholder farmers share in the gains should serve as the core criterion for assessing integration outcomes, and that progress should be advanced in a coordinated manner through precision-oriented technology supply, cultivation of actors' digital literacy, innovation in benefit-linkage mechanisms and optimization of institutional safeguards.
evidence_items.title: Mechanisms and Pathways of Artificial Intelligence–Driven Rural Industrial Integration
